items.title: How Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state
items.description: As abductions go, few have been more brazen. Alan Jalloh was with two friends outside Goodies supermarket, frantic as usual with late afternoon shoppers. Rush hour in downtown Freetown, Sierra Leone’s capital, was under way with familiar gusto. A black Toyota Rav4 forced its way through the Peninsula highway traffic. Witnesses describe burly white men leaping out, yanking on balaclavas. Jalloh, 40, seemed to freeze. As did his two friends, one a famous Freetown footballer. All three were dragged into the waiting SUV. None of them have been seen since. Two days later, on 25 October 2025, another three men disappeared. Within a week, nine people had been seized from the city’s streets, most in broad daylight. They were dismembered, police sources were told. At least one was beheaded. An officer investigating Jalloh’s abduction, says: “They were exterminated to hide the truth.” No bodies have been found. Five months after Jalloh disappeared, an ageing cargo ship, the Arconian, left Freetown. By May, it was navigating savage seas 100 miles off the coast of Morocco when Spanish civil guards boarded. Lucas Fernández*, clutching his assault rifle on the ship’s lower deck, stumbled across figures in the Arconian’s darkened cargo hold. Fernández raised his gun, finger on the trigger. A man pointed an assault rifle back at him. Time stood still. Fernández says the man became agitated, yelling in English, incomprehensible above the storm outside. “It was crazy,” Fernández says. Within minutes, he and his fellow officers had disarmed six gunmen found hiding in the bowels of the ship. Nearby, were 1,279 bales of cocaine wrapped in plastic; weighing between 30 and 45 tonnes, it is the largest amount of the drug ever seized. Seventeen days later, the audience at Oxford University rose to applaud the guest speaker. Julius Maada Bio had nailed it once again. His address – eulogising robust leadership – was the latest in a whirlwind year for the president of Sierra Leone. The chair of Ecowas – the Economic Union of West African States, a region home to more than 400 million people, Bio is among the most influential African voices in the UN. The EU sees Bio as one of its most reliable allies in Africa and has a long history of showering the impoverished country with aid stretching back more than 45 years. But the most important figure in Sierra Leone is not this ambitious politician, but the man who ordered the abduction of Jalloh; the man responsible for the Arconian’s monumental cocaine stash. A man called Jos Leijdekkers. He also happens to be Bio’s son-in-law. At 35, Leijdekkers is Europe’s pre-eminent cocaine baron. Intelligence assessments credit the Dutchman with importing volumes vast enough to repeatedly crash Europe’s cocaine market. Last year, he halved the drug’s wholesale price. Multiple intelligence sources confirm he has also transformed Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state. “It is state capture by a criminal network on a scale never seen,” says a western official. At least 14 people have been killed inside Sierra Leone on Leijdekkers’ orders. High-ranking police are believed to have been murdered on his say-so. Officers have fled the country fearing they will be next. “If you get in his way, he wipes you out,” says an intelligence source. Like most, they spoke on condition of anonymity, aware of Leijdekkers’ capacity to reach those who cross him. Sierra Leone’s fate is a tale of western duplicity. Despite detailed intelligence of the extraordinary volumes of cocaine being exported to Europe, the EU continued to woo Bio and his government. The UN did the same: overlooking its own evidence. And intelligence sources warn that Leijdekkers’ network is rapidly expanding. “The entire west Africa region is at risk,” says a Dutch official. Leijdekkers’ prodigious transcontinental network brings deadly violence. Dozens of his gunmen descended on a sleepy Dutch village last month intent on retribution. A European police source said: “We’ve had cocaine disputes before, but nothing like this. We’ve entered a new era.” The first recorded sighting of Leijdekkers in west Africa came in October 2022. A six-vehicle convoy thundered down Aberdeen Road, towards Lumley beach, leaving Freetown traffic police baffled. No one had briefed they were expecting VIPs. “‘The convoy was bigger than our president’s,” says one officer. Unaware of Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker, Freetown police were sufficiently concerned to begin surveillance on the mysterious convoy, which had stopped outside the Sky Bar, a nightlife institution in the city. At 4am, the group were trailed to a waterfront house near Hamilton beach. There, the covert surveillance team were stunned: revellers included their own bosses. At the time, western intelligence agencies had no idea of Leijdekkers’ whereabouts. One of Europe’s most wanted men had simply vanished. For years, authorities had tracked his rise in the Dutch underworld, watching how the local hitman from the well-heeled town of Prinsenbeek accrued key contacts for transatlantic cocaine shipments. When Dutch intelligence traced Leijdekkers to Sierra Leone in 2024, he had created something remarkable: a sprawling cocaine empire from scratch. “He’s very adept at adaptation, cultivating ties,” says an official. “A new country, but he won over its most influential people.” That included marrying the president’s daughter, Agnes Bio, and starting a family. Sierra Leone’s top officials partied with the moneyed new guy. Immigration chiefs secured him a diplomatic passport. The person whose job it was to investigate cocaine traffickers became a drinking buddy. Leijdekkers’ wealth corrupted. According to intelligence, he was generating a $150m (£113m) monthly profit – greater than the running cost of Sierra Leone’s entire state. Hundreds of people were on his payroll, say sources, including senior military and police figures. But what Leijdekkers coveted most was Freetown’s seaport: the Queen Elizabeth II Quay, perfectly sited between cocaine-producing South America and Europe’s booming markets. In August 2023, his wife’s uncle, Yankuba Bio, became head of the port. Yankuba Bio denies a close relationship with “any individual called or identified as Jos Leijdekkers”.Sources, though, say port officials on Leijdekkers’s payroll make $2,000 a month – more than 30 times the national average . In January 2025,the Dutch sent an extradition request to Sierra Leone for the fugitive, who had been sentenced in absentia to more than 100 years in prison for crimes including attempted murder. Sierra Leone denied knowing the man. For Leijdekkers, it was a defining moment: he had state protection. His confidence culminated in the arrival into Freetown’s port on 18 April of the Arconian, a green cargo vessel the length of a football pitch. Over the next four days, about 30 tonnes of cocaine were hauled onboard, according to western intelligence. “From experience, the maximum you can hide is eight tonnes. Thirty tonnes says you’re operating in plain sight,” says a UN agent. Yankuba Bio says such claims are “false, completely untrue and without foundation” adding that the port “does not engage in or facilitate the export” of cocaine. On 26 April, a cryptic tip-off electrified European investigators. An unidentified vessel had left west Africa carrying 18 tonnes of cocaine, the second-largest such cargo identified in Europe. Within 70 hours, the Arconian had been identified. At 8pm on 1 May, with the vessel pitching in brutal, black seas, Fernández, of Spain’s civil guard central operational unit, was first onboard. Having arrested the 23-strong Filipino crew, the officer spotted a gun lying on the deck. “We started to search more deeply,” says Fernández. After his team stumbled across the six-strong paramilitary detail guarding the cocaine, it became chillingly evident the gunmen had orders to kill anyone who threatened Leijdekkers’ drugs. They had no idea Fernández was a police officer. “They thought we were an organisation come to rob the drugs,” he says. “It was very tense. Anyone – them, us – might have fired.” It took interminable seconds for Leijdekkers’ men to appreciate the truth. “They knew then it would be worse to open fire.” The Arconian seizure shattered previous understanding of cocaine trafficking. Firstly, Leijdekkers appeared certain that his €812m (£687m) cargo would reach Europe. No attempt was made to conceal the drugs. “There was a 60-metre-long corridor full of it,” says Fernández. Such nonchalance corroborated intelligence assessments that Leijdekkers had repeatedly flooded Europe with shipments, utilising a vast narco fleet and driving the wholesale cocaine price to a record low. In the weeks before the raid, the Arconian completely changed its identity. Analysis for the Guardian by the maritime AI company Windward tracked at least three “suspicious” vessels from Freetown in the months before the Arconian. All rebranded themselves before leaving Sierra Leone. In January this year, a cargo boat changed its registration details just before arriving in Freetown. After a month, it left for an unspecified destination. On 15 March, the vessel loitered off the Canary Islands for four hours. Investigators say the Arconian intended to linger off the Spanish archipelago, offloading the cocaine to a flotilla of speedboats. Spanish police at the port of Santa Cruz de Tenerife, Spain, in January, guarding the what was then a record seizure of the drug. Photograph: Ramón de la Rocha/EPA Last Christmas Eve, another suspicious ship altered its name, flag and identifying traits when anchored off Freetown. With no destination declared, it left on Christmas Day. Approaching the Canary Islands on 9 January, it slowed and remained there for 13 hours before heading to Libya, which was also the Arconian’s stated destination. Exactly the same pattern was observed with a ship leaving Freetown on 15 December, too. Another eight vessels with near-identical traits to the Arconian have departed Freetown for Libya via the Canary Islands since 2024. These include the White Labeille, which left Freetown in November 2024, was tracked off the Canary Islands and later “went dark”, switching off locator devices. Four months earlier, the White Eagle departed Sierra Leone before going dark off Morocco and being mysteriously abandoned. On the same day, another vessel – the White Arrow – was discarded in Libya with its Filipino crew, weeks after leaving Freetown. Other ships were found abandoned close to Freetown. One trawler, Sky 777, ran aground on Lumley Beach last year. No one has claimed it. Months later, the Agios Basseterre drifted on to nearby Hamilton beach. Witnesses described white men hurriedly retrieving packages from the boat. It, too, was never claimed. As investigators pored over the Arconian, Sierra Leonean authorities claimed its cargo originated from a mystery maritime transfer. However, analysis for the Guardian of its final voyage by Lloyd’s List Intelligence confirmed that the ship’s speed was consistent. There were no stops for a ship-to-ship transfer. Something else did not seem right. Usually, the loss of even a modest cocaine cargo unleashes a wave of underworld violence. Intelligence agencies waited for the bloodshed. Two days after the Arconian’s seizure, Leijdekkers chaired a Freetown summit to pinpoint what had gone wrong. Who gave the tip-off? Did he have a mole? But no violence followed. “Mind-boggling amounts of cocaine had gone,” says a police source, “but Leijdekkers behaved like nothing had happened. Extraordinary.” Perhaps Alan Jalloh underestimated Leijdekkers? Or maybe he was blinded by greed? Either way, intelligence indicates he was seen to have “betrayed” the Dutch fugitive over a cocaine deal. Police investigating the kidnapping made a swift breakthrough. Officers tracked down the black Toyota SUV. “We recognised it from our surveillance work on Leijdekkers,” says one. Three kidnappers were arrested, but before they could be questioned, senior officers intervened. “They were released the same day,” says a source. The investigating team’s caseload snowballed. Two days later, inquiries prompted a police raid on a Freetown warehouse. Inside were two teenagers and the property owner, guarding blocks of cocaine. Halfway through the arrest, 40 armed troops turned up. At gunpoint, police were ordered to release the suspects. “Officers were told to leave everything with the military. Nobody saw those boys again,” says a police source. Over the following days, other people went missing, including the owner of a Lumley beach bar. A name linking the disappeared kept cropping up: Leijdekkers. Detectives, though, felt their inquiry was increasingly thwarted. The lead investigator was abruptly transferred: Jalloh’s family could no longer contact them. Nine people had disappeared, yet not a single police statement was issued. Such silence is even more striking because Jalloh, a shopkeeper, was related to Sierra Leone’s vice-president, and kidnapped alongside Alusine “Bokay” Koroma, a lauded Sierra Leonean international footballer. Asked for details of its investigation, Sierra Leone police did not respond. The military also declined to comment. Westernintelligence reports, though, are unequivocal: Leijdekkers’ enforcers murdered Jalloh. “His mercenaries were supported by the police and military,” says one report. Witness statements reveal that hours before he was abducted, troops visited Jalloh’s Freetown Liquor Mart and looted its contents. Some of those kidnapped, police learned, were buried at Freetown’s police cemetery. “Reliable sources say they were sliced with a power saw while alive. A pit was dug, the bodies dissolved with chemicals and concreted over,” said a Sierra Leonean police officer. Another source with knowledge of the burials informed investigators that a “head was missing”. Other deaths occurred, such as John Conteh, who worked at Freetown’s port, checking container seals at the quayside. Intelligence sources reveal Conteh began “monitoring and inspecting containers” linked to Leijdekkers. At about 1am on 2 June 2024, Conteh was crushed in work machinery. In the commercially sensitive heart of one of west Africa’s most critical ports, his death was apparently not caught on CCTV. Conteh, who worked for Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC), the world’s largest shipping group, is the only MSC employee to have died in Freetown since it started operations there 14 years ago. Eight days after Conteh’s death, Sierra Leonean authorities concluded the incident was a “work-related accident”. MSC declined to comment, referring to port authority statements. Sierra Leone police similarly chose not to respond. Western intelligence believe Conteh died in “suspicious circumstances”. A covert picture of Leijdekkers, allegedly taken last year in the Aberdeen area of Freetown Even high-ranking police officers are at risk. On 8 April 2023, Supt Matthew “Boyka” Banya was in a marked police car near Makeni’s famous clock tower. Banya was adjusting to the northern city, having been ousted from Freetown after allegedly falling foul of Leijdekkers’ network. An assassin shot Banya in his vehicle at point-blank range. “Boyka wanted to expose Leijdekkers so an assailant was sent,” a Sierra Leonean police source claims. The president himself urged police action but no killer was caught. “There was no proper investigation. They let it go,” added the source. Justice campaigners claim they were “obstructed” by the authorities. Police would not comment. Such unsolved killings have chilled the country. Residents describe a climate of fear. “Targeted assassinations, cover-ups and impunity. We are terrified,” says one local politician. Most feared are the “commandos”, Leijdekkers’ Turkish, Dutch and Serbian bodyguards, armed with pistols and assault rifles. Journalists attempting to document Leijdekkers risk arrest, as happened to the Dutch reporter Sophie van Leeuwen, who travelled to Freetown last year. A 24/7 police surveillance operation was instigated. At one point, officers watched her drive past Leijdekkers as he drank in the Sky Bar. On her sixth day in Freetown, she was detained for several days on spying charges before being released. Her media files were deleted. Politicians are similarly silenced. Abdul Kargbo, leader of the opposition, alleges that he was threatened after raising trafficking concerns. “They sent people to advise me to stay off [the issue],” he says. Leijdekkers shows little sign of lying low, openly enjoying his favourite nightspots, Scarlet, Lor and the Sky Bar. But observers report an increase in security; more armed guards, more lookouts and increasingly rigorous counter-surveillance. Drivers are frequently rotated. His fleet of vehicles are routinely changed. When Leijdekkers makes a journey, reconnaissance teams are dispatched 24 hours in advance. “He seems more paranoid,” says a source. His caution might be valid. Twice, Dutch special forces have been positioned off the west African coast preparing to seize him. Aborted at the last minute, the operations will have jangled nerves. “His biggest fear is a mole,” says a Sierra Leonean source. Several trusted lieutenants aside, Leijdekkers’ business is largely a one-man show. “It makes his network difficult to infiltrate; it can absorb the arrest of senior figures while easily getting rid of juniors.” His willingness to eradicate any perceived weak links can be seen, sources allege, in the deaths of a specialist police unit. Leijdekkers, they claim, feared the team knew too much, including where Jalloh was buried. Two months after the shopowner disappeared, a police vehicle crashed, killing three officers. The official account was that it was an accident. Days later, a fourth officer of the unit was found hanged. “His family knows their son would not hang himself. No investigation was mounted,” says a police source. Leijdekkers’ arrival has also brought a surge in cocaine’s popularity among Freetown’s middle classes, particularly the Lumley beach nightclubs. The drug’s street price is the lowest in west Africa. Abubakar Sesay, 32, a cocaine addict in Freetown, says dealers operate with political protection: “The bulk is mainly for export to Europe, but a small quantity is sold locally through criminal networks facilitating the trafficking trade.” Experts already warn that cocaine poses a serious public health concern, particularly if processed into cheaper crack cocaine. “We’re already seeing overdoses,” says a drugs campaigner. Despite its relatively low street price, the drug’s wider popularity in Sierra Leone is still limited by its cost, as nearly half of the population live in extreme poverty. Very few people benefit from Leijdekkers’ largesse, with sources estimating only a “few hundred” of the country’s nine million people share in the profits. Yet cocaine has warped the country’s economy. One dish at Lor restaurant can cost £270 – five months’ pay for the average Sierra Leonean. A slew of luxury car showrooms line Wilkinson Road; new apartments abound. “My driver showed me a huge multi-storey building built by a police officer. Not a regional commander – a traffic cop!” says the politician. Fresh construction linked to Leijdekkers is emerging across west Africa. Operating bases have been established within Liberia, Guinea Bissau and now Ghana. Using diplomatic passports, Leijdekkers and his men roam the region with ease. Witnesses describe Liberian police applauding his convoy as it crossed the border. On 21 July, the biggest drugs bust in Liberia’s history was announced when almost 4 tonnes of Leijdekkers’ cocaine, worth £235m, was found near its capital, Monrovia. The previous day, sources say Leijdekkers returned to Freetown from Liberia. They also recognised the man arrested with the Monrovia cocaine, who was seen with Leijdekkers in Freetown. Leijdekkers “frequently” visits Guinea Bissau, courting the junta that seized power last November. There is scrutiny, too, in Ghana where last month several of Leijdekkers’ network were arrested. As gifts go, they caught the eye. On 23 June 2026, EU officials gave two sleek speedboats to Bio’s government at a ceremony in Freetown. The vessels were for the same military co-opted by Leijdekkers to help tackle drug trafficking – one of many EU offerings made despite detailed warnings over Leijdekkers’ influence in Sierra Leone. In a deal signed before Leijdekkers arrived in Freetown, Brussels sanctioned a €352m aid package running until 2027. So far, €245m has been paid. In August 2024 – weeks after Dutch intelligence confirmed Bio’s government was harbouring Europe’s chief cocaine importer – the EU agreed to give an extra €90m to Sierra Leone. In January 2025, another €35m was unlocked at a Freetown meeting with EU officials. Other deals involved tens of millions of EU taxpayers’ money paid directly into Sierra Leone’s treasury. After the Arconian seizure, on 9 June 2026, Brussels opened the European chamber of commerce in Freetown to boost investment. Its inaugural president was the Sierra Leonean head of the shipping company whose employee John Conteh died at Freetown’s port. Strengthening democracy was a core ambition of European investment in Sierra Leone. Since Leijdekkers arrival, the EU has spent €5.6m on the issue: not enough to prevent recent allegations that he financed $100,000 bribes in an attempt to corrupt its electoral system. The Dutch justice minister, David van Weel, exasperated with Bio’s refusal to extradite Leijdekkers, wants Brussels to freeze development aid to Freetown. To date, just €18m of funding has been suspended. Agnes Bio, Leijdekkers’ wife, addressing the UN security council in 2024. Photograph: UN In summer 2024, as evidence indicated that Bio’s government was protecting Leijdekkers, Sierra Leone assumed the rotating presidency of the UN security council. In June 2025, after becoming chair of Ecowas, Bio led a committee demanding a permanent African seat on the security council. The UN body, which is mandated to impose sanctions on a country controlled by a drug lord, seems unwilling to target one of its lamentably few African voices. “There was no appetite. Leijdekkers never came up,” says a European diplomat. Bio doubled down on his statesman persona. Ten days after the Arconian was seized, he met the French president, Emmanuel Macron, before flying to London for his speech at Oxford. In September, Bio addressed world leaders at the UN general assembly with a speech on “restoring trust”. A New York meeting with Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, saw Bio’s economic policies feted. Anti-narcotics investigators were gobsmacked. Even Leijdekkers’ 32-year-old wife, Agnes, is accredited to Sierra Leone’s UN mission in New York. In London, where Bio’s wife, Fatima, until recently had a council flat, a dedicated team is investigating Leijdekkers’ sprawling UK connections. Sharing daily briefings with their Dutch counterparts, Britain’s National Crime Agency has identified interlinked trafficking networks. “Intelligence is telling us that he’s linked to an awful lot of things. We have a number [of UK cocaine importations] we think he was involved in,” said a UK source. The British government has not aired any concerns over Bio’s government. It resembled a scene from Sinaloa, the Mexican region where drug cartels use brazen violence to subjugate the state and send a show of force. It was the quiet Dutch village of Overasselt where, on 1 September this year, dozens of heavily armed men descended. Leijdekkers’ hastily assembled “narco-army” opened fire on a rural warehouse, killing a security guard and, when police arrived, seriously wounding two officers. In the pre-dawn chaos, 34 of the narco trafficker’s foot soldiers were arrested. A cache of high-velocity weapons was found nearby. For Europe’s police, it was the realisation of a long-dreaded nightmare: Latin America’s cartel-style violence had arrived. Leijdekkers attack on Overasselt was completely out of character. Intelligence updates had long chronicled a trafficking network characterised by meticulous paperwork and finely tuned logistics to remain under the radar. Overasselt was the precise opposite. “He’s getting desperate,” a Dutch police source believes. Having lost €812m on the Arconian, the Overasselt raid was prompted by the loss on 29 August of 1.2 tonnes of cocaine near the French-Spanish border. Leijdekkers believed a rival had nabbed it. Within two days, he and associates had recruited for this outlandish raid. But Leijdekkers was wrong. It was police, in fact, who had intercepted the €50m cargo. Days later, the fugitive faced another egregious blow when police officers confirmed they had caught Leijdekkers’ chief financier, a senior operator in a clandestine money transfer system dubbed “Dubai bank”. Since the Arconian was intercepted, Leijdekkers has lost up to 12 shipments – and the wholesale price of cocaine in Europe has risen from €12,000 to €22,000 a kilo. His cumulative losses, police believe, have left him in debt to the Colombian Cali cartel. He also faces a gigantic monthly payroll inside Sierra Leone. A cornered Leijdekkers is a dangerous proposition. Having outlasted former accomplices, such as the alleged crime boss Daniel Kinahan, recently extradited from Dubai to Ireland, and the convicted Moroccan-Dutch trafficker Ridouan Taghi, sentenced to life in prison in 2024, Leijdekkers retains extensive influence within the sprawling criminal ecosystem in north Africa and Europe, the so-called Mocro mafia. Police sources, who once insisted Freetown would “never, ever” extradite their wealthy guest, are now wondering if that might change. And for the Bio family, international pressure is escalating. Van Weel, the Netherlands’ justice and security minister, said work was under way to “sanction” individuals linked to Leijdekkers. The president’s office declined to comment, though there is no suggestion he is implicated in any suspected illegal activity linked to Leijdekkers. Leijdekkers’ lawyer dismissed the allegations as “politically driven”. A subsequent statement read: “My client wants you to know that the information you got from anonymous sources is complete nonsense, probably nourished by the Dutch authorities and therefore not fit for publication.” Sierra Leone stands on the brink, along with the rest of west Africa. A regional narco-economy, where fragile states are overwhelmed by entrenched corruption and ruthless criminal networks, remains a distinct possibility. Like Jalloh, Leijdekkers may disappear from Freetown. He will probably surface elsewhere to assemble a fresh empire. “There’s no sign of him retiring,” says a police source. “Every day, the guy’s growing his wings, expanding his network.” This article was amended on 15 October 2026 to correct a number of misspellings of Jos Leijdekkers’ surname and the spelling of the village of Overasselt.

items.title: Une embarcation transportant 191 candidats à l’immigration clandestine prise en charge par la garde côte mauritanienne
items.description: La Garde côtière mauritanienne a annoncé ce mercredi avoir intercepté un bateau en provenance de Barni, au Sénégal, transportant 191 candidats à l'immigration clandestine de différentes nationalités. Lors d’un point presse, la Garde côtière a indiqué que ses forces avaient intercepté l’embarcation à 12 h 00, heure universelle, dans le cadre de ses missions de surveillance, de sauvetage et de protection des vies humaines dans les eaux relevant de la souveraineté mauritanienne. Elle a ajouté que les passagers de l’embarcation comprenaient 170 Sénégalais, 15 Guinéens, 3 Gambiennes, deux Mauritaniens et un ressortissant ivoirien. Selon le communiqué, le groupe sénégalais comprend deux femmes et 12 mineurs, tandis que le groupe guinéen compte 13 femmes et deux mineurs ; quant aux trois Gambiennes, il s’agit de mineures. La Garde côtière a précisé que cette opération s’inscrit dans le cadre de ses efforts continus visant à surveiller les eaux territoriales, à mener des opérations de sauvetage et à lutter contre l’immigration clandestine, tout en veillant à protéger les vies humaines et à traiter les situations humanitaires conformément aux procédures en vigueur.

items.title: PM Shehbaz vows to strengthen Maldives ties for 'all time to come'; 20 MoUs signed
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday vowed to strengthen bilateral relations with the Maldives, as the two countries signed 20 memorandums of understanding (MoUs) during the visit of President Dr Mohamed Muizzu. Muizzu arrived in Islamabad on Tuesday on a three-day visit at the invitation of PM Shehbaz Sharif. The visit marks the first by a Maldivian president to Pakistan in 11 years, and comes as the two countries celebrate the 60th anniversary of their diplomatic relations, established in 1966. Addressing a joint press stakeout following the signing of 20 wide-ranging MoUs, PM Shehbaz said, “There is no doubt that the two countries [will] keep on strengthening these relations for all time to come.” The premier extended a “very warm welcome” to the visiting dignitary and his delegation. PM Shehbaz expressed his “warmest greetings and heartfelt affection to the people of Dhivehi Raajje, the land of islands, a nation whose spirit is as vast as the ocean that surrounds it,” hailing 60 years of diplomatic ties between the two countries. The prime minister noted that he and Muizzu, in their bilateral and delegation-level talks, discussed “all important issues which have direct bearing between our two brotherly countries and of course, regional and international issues”. “I am very happy to announce that we had a wonderful session, very productive and very fruitful discussions,” he remarked. PM Shehbaz noted that the conversations encompassed “economic and trade relations, our strategic defence cooperation, our support for training of our brothers and sisters from Maldives in Pakistan in various walks of life; police, defence, education, health and many other” fields. The prime minister went on to announce that both sides had agreed to raise their bilateral trade from $13.9 million — “just a fraction of our potential” — to $200m in the next two years. Highlighting that the two South Asian countries had “very strong” relations, coupled with a “long list of mutual achievements”, PM Shehbaz said both sides noted that their ties “do not reflect the true strength of our economic cooperation”. Thanking Muizzu for his “personal support in this behalf”, the premier went on to announce that Islamabad would support Malé in promoting the plantation of 5m trees in the Maldives by providing 100,000 olive cuttings and 100,000 seeds of various plant species within a mutually decided timeframe. Referring to the MoUs signed, he affirmed that he “will be very happy to personally work with [Muizzu] to translate these written MoUs into action with prompt decision-making and speedy implementation”. The prime minister declared that Pakistan was “absolutely ready to provide technical expertise to various segments of our mutual cooperation and, above all, Pakistan is very happy to learn that Maldives is moving forward speedily to establish data centres in other places”. “This is great news, and as a matter of good luck, Pakistan has also attained a reasonable level of expertise and professional capability in this field,” he added, noting that the country had set up data centres in various locations. He offered Pakistan’s “experience and our professional capabilities in this behalf” to the Maldives. PM Shehbaz noted that a large number of Maldivian students were receiving education in Pakistani universities and colleges, particularly in the field of healthcare, and that 250 Pakistani doctors and other paramedics were serving in the Maldives. “This shall continue in future with bigger numbers so that whatever requirements you have, we as a brotherly country would be more than happy to fulfil those requirements willingly and with utmost sincerity of purpose,” the prime minister said. Speaking on international developments, PM Shehbaz commended the Maldives’ “unwavering” support for the Palestinian cause, adding that Islamabad remains fully committed to the Palestinians’ right of self-determination and the establishment of an independent state of Palestine. The premier further said he briefed Muizzu on Pakistan’s principled position on occupied Jammu and Kashmir, declaring Islamabad’s support for a peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with the relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions. “Till they have won their struggle and gotten the right of self-determination, Pakistan shall continue to support them diplomatically and, of course, support them at all international forums till they become an independent sovereign country as per UNSC resolutions, and their sacrifice will not go to waste at all,” he said. The prime minister also expressed Pakistan’s “serious concern” over India’s decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance in April 2025, pointing out that it was a violation of an international binding treaty. “Pakistan’s position is loud and clear and beyond an array of doubt; legally binding treaties must be respected and shared water resources must never be weaponised or used as an instrument of political pressure or blackmailing,” he stated. PM Shehbaz said Pakistan has made it “abundantly clear at various forums ”, including the UN General Assembly last month, that water was a “red line” for the country. “Waterflows in any canal or ocean, sea or straits, carries trade, commerce, message of prosperity and progress, and not threats, confrontations and conflicts,” he said. “Water is a lifeline for humanity […] so this should be known to all and sundry that any violation in this behalf will be regarded by Pakistan as an act of war,” the prime minister warned. Concluding his remarks, PM Shehbaz said Muizzu’s visit had given Pakistan-Maldives relations “new purpose and new momentum”. He remarked, “The same ocean that touches the shores of Karachi and Gwadar embraces the islands of the Maldives. “For centuries, its waves have carried traders, scholars and travellers between our lands. Today, they carry the renewed promise of our wonderful friendship whose finest chapters are yet to be written.” In his comments, Muizzu appreciated PM Shehbaz, the government and people of Pakistan for “their exceptional warmth and gracious hospitality”. He added that his visit coming on the 60-year mark of Pakistan-Maldives diplomatic relations made it “particularly significant”. The 60 years have been marked by warmth, friendship and shared perspectives, he said. “This visit takes place after a decade-long interval. It offers us an important opportunity not simply to celebrate the friendship of the past but to define the partnership of the future,” Muizzu said. Stressing on the close relations between the two countries, he said, “Only two such longstanding friends could have talked so widely and agreed on so much about our future together”. Muizzu said, for him, the talks represented a “clear shared ambition to move the Maldives-Pakistan partnership into a new era”. He said the discussions encompassed several sectors including trade and investment; health and education; environment, fisheries and agriculture; youth and sports; policing and defence; training and capacity-building; and tourism. The Maldivian president said he was pleased about the signing of 20 MOUs. “These memoranda will open new avenues for cooperation among multiple sectors, but agreements are meaningful only when they produce results. Our next step, of course, is to translate these understandings into tangible opportunities and meaningful benefits for the people of both nations.” Muizzu also said he endorsed the goal to take the two countries’ bilateral trade quantum from $13m to $200m in two years. “The Maldives and Pakistan are worlds of untapped potential for each other,” the Maldivian president said. He reaffirmed that the two countries would take a “firm step in the right direction”, adding that Thursday’s business forum would provide an opportunity to bring together business leaders, inventors and innovators from both countries to turn the friendship into mutually beneficial investments. He said he was encouraged by the discussions to establish direct flights between Pakistan and the Maldives, adding that direct flights would help support tourism as well. He further said that the two countries’ leaders saw “considerable potential in halal and Muslim-friendly tourism”. Moreover, Muizzu appreciated Pakistan’s scholarships and placements for Maldivian students, adding that the leaders would broaden the opportunities further, especially in artificial intelligence, digitisation and future technologies as well as health. “We want our next generation to be prepared for the future and be prepared to shape that future.” Muizzu stressed that climate change was “not an abstract environmental concern” for the Maldives, but “it is a direct challenge to our security, our development and our future”. He welcomed cooperation with Pakistan in areas of climate resilience, conservation, sustainable waste management and renewable energy. He thanked PM Shehbaz for his announcement of donations to help the Maldives plant 5m trees in five years. “Our nations share a commitment to advancing common interests through constructive engagements.” He said the Maldives remained committed to revitalising the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, adding that “rebuilding trust, encouraging meaningful dialogue and strengthening mutual understanding are essential to unlocking the full potential of regional cooperation”. He further expressed the Maldives’ “unequivocal and steadfast solidarity” with Palestinians and their “legitimate right to self-determination”. Muizzu also commended Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts “to promote dialogue, de-escalation, humanitarian assistance and a just and lasting peace” in the Middle East. Concluding his remarks, he said, “For 60 years, Pakistan has stood as a trusted friend of the Maldives.” The two countries have now agreed to “build a new era of partnership on the foundations of our six decades of friendship”, he said. The Maldivian president was later conferred with an honorary doctorate in politics by the International Islamic University Islamabad, with PM Shehbaz noting that the degree recognised Muizzu’s “sagacious and wise leadership and your great public service to your people in the Maldives”. 20 MoUs signed Pakistan and the Maldives on Wednesday signed a series of MoUs aimed at deepening bilateral relations in multiple sectors, including defence, IT, cybersecurity, health, education, social protection, agriculture and tourism, among others. PM Shehbaz and Muizzu were present at the ceremony where representatives from both sides exchanged the pre-signed documents. The two countries signed an MoU on cooperation in the fields of information technology, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, digital skills, and technology and innovation. An MoU was inked to strengthen cooperation in combating illicit trafficking and abuse of narcotic drugs. The two sides also signed an MoU on social protection as well as on health cooperation and between Maldives Food and Drug Authority and the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan. Both nations also signed MoUs focused on the recruitment of health professionals, strengthening defence ties and maritime security cooperation. An MoU was signed to boost agriculture cooperation, besides another one on promoting fisheries cooperation. To promote ties in technical and vocational education, an MoU on collaboration to promote technical and vocational education and training was signed, while another MoU was inked to promote educational cooperation. The representatives of Pakistan and the Maldives also exchanged MoUs on cooperation in the field of youth and sports development, air connectivity, tourism and in the field of arts, culture and heritage. The MoUs were signed between the National College of Policy and Law Enforcement of the Maldives Police Service and National Police Academy, Islamabad; Civil Service Commission of Maldives and the Federal Public Service Commission of Pakistan; and Civil Service Commission of Maldives and Civil Service Academy (CSA) of Pakistan. In order to boost commercial engagement, an MoU was signed between the Maldives State Trading Organisation (STO) and Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) for cooperation in trade of agriculture commodities, food and other products, besides signing another pact aimed at boosting cooperation in the field of environment. Prior to the MoU signing ceremony, Muizzi was welcomed at the Prime Minister House with a guard of honour. He held introductions with federal ministers while PM Shehbaz greeted the Maldivian delegation. According to a statement by PM Office (PMO), the prime minister extended a “warm welcome to the esteemed guest”, followed by a guard of honour by smartly turned-out contingents of all three armed forces. The visiting dignitary also planted a sapling at PM House, and prayers were offered for the progress and prosperity of both countries. An earlier statement issued by the Foreign Office (FO) said Muizzu will meet President Asif Ali Zardari and will also hold “restricted and delegation-level” talks with PM Shehbaz. A Pakistan-Maldives Business Forum will also be held during the visit to promote interaction between the two countries’ business communities and explore opportunities for trade and investment. President Zardari calls for stronger bilateral economic cooperation President Zardari also met his Maldivian counterpart at the President’s House in Islamabad, where he emphasised the need to translate the political goodwill between the two countries into “greater trade, investment, connectivity and people-to-people exchanges”. According to a press release by the President’s secretariat, he also reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to supporting Maldives in education, healthcare, human resource development, social protection and sustainable development. “The two leaders reviewed bilateral relations and discussed ways to strengthen cooperation in areas of mutual interest,” the statement said. President Zardari reaffirmed the importance Pakistan attaches to its “longstanding fraternal relations” with the Maldives, highlighting that Muizzu’s state visit coincided with the 60-year anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries and provided “fresh momentum” to the bilateral partnership. He also recalled Pakistan’s contributions to the development of the Maldives, including the Parliament building and the School of Medicine in Malé. The press release added that both leaders expressed satisfaction over the positive trajectory of bilateral relations and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in areas of mutual interest. They recognised the disproportionate impact of climate change on vulnerable countries, particularly small island developing states and climate-vulnerable developing economies. “President Zardari expressed Pakistan’s readiness to deepen cooperation with Maldives in climate resilience, environmental protection and sustainable development, including support for President Muizzu’s Five Million Tree Initiative,” the statement said. Additionally, the leaders exchanged views on regional and international developments and underscored the importance of “dialogue, diplomacy, sovereign equality, mutual respect and peaceful resolution of disputes”, it said. They also reaffirmed their support for the rights of the Palestinian people and the establishment of an independent and sovereign State of Palestine. According to the statement, Muizzu was accompanied by Iruthisham Adam, Minister of Foreign Affairs; Hassan Rasheed, Minister of Defence and National Service; Ali Ihusaan, Minister of Homeland Security, Labour and Technology; Mohamed Saeed, Minister of Economic Development, Transport and Trade; and Mohamed Thoha, High Commissioner of the Republic of Maldives. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Maritime Minister Junaid Anwar, Senators Sherry Rehman and Saleem Mandviwala, former federal minister MNA Naveed Qamar, the foreign secretary, and the High Commissioner of Pakistan to the Maldives were also present, it added. The meeting was followed by a state banquet hosted by President Zardari in honour of President Muizzu and his accompanying delegation. It was attended, among others, by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif; Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir; Senate Chairman Syed Yousuf Raza Gilani; National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq; Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf; Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu; and Commander National Strategic Command, General Syed Aamer Raza, as well as members of the Federal Cabinet, Parliament and diplomatic corps. Meeting with Dar Earlier in the day, DPM Dar called on Muizzu, welcoming him and his delegation to Pakistan, the FO said on X. Dar “underscored the importance of expanding bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade, investment, education, climate change and tourism”, the FO said. DPM Dar also welcomed the Maldivian business delegation in the Maldives-Pakistan Business Forum and “expressed hope that B2B engagements would yield concrete trade and investment opportunities”. Muizzu, speaking to Dar, “expressed Maldives’ desire to deepen its close relations with Pakistan and explore new avenues of mutually beneficial cooperation”, the FO said. Separately, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry held a meeting with Maldivian Minister for Homeland Security Ali Ihusan and exchanged views on enhancing bilateral relations and cooperation between the two countries, a statement by the interior ministry said. According to the statement, the two agreed to promote cooperation on immigration and to curb human smuggling and organised crime. It quoted Chaudhry as saying: “Pakistan values sharing experiences and security cooperation with friendly countries to promote peace and stability in the region. Pakistan wants to strengthen bilateral cooperation with the Maldives in the areas of law enforcement and internal security.” He stressed the need for cooperation between the two sides to tackle the challenges of illegal immigration and human smuggling and assured the visiting dignitary on Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s behalf of “all-possible assistance for enhancing bilateral cooperation”. Last month, the Maldives’ parliamentary speaker Abdul Raheem Abdullah met with Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir in Rawalpindi. In 2015 , former Maldivian president Abdulla Yameen Abdul Gayoom undertook a two-day state visit to Pakistan on May 6-7 at the invitation of then-PM Nawaz Sharif.

items.title: No mineworker should suffer under contract mining policy – Government
items.description: The government has assured mineworkers that no employee should suffer a reduction in wages, benefits or conditions of service as mining companies transition from owner mining to contract mining. The Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources says workers employed by mining contractors must receive salaries, wages, allowances, benefits and other incentives equivalent to those enjoyed by owner mining workers performing comparable work before the transition. The assurance forms part of additional policy measures announced by the Ministry to guide the implementation of Ghana’s contract mining policy and address concerns about its potential impact on workers. In a statement signed by the Ministry’s Director of Communications, Zambaga Rufai Saminu, the government said it had taken account of concerns raised by the Ghana Mineworkers Union, human resource experts and other stakeholders over the possible effects of the transition on workers’ remuneration and welfare. The Ministry and the Minerals Commission have been holding consultations with the Union’s leadership, industry experts and other relevant stakeholders. According to the statement, the engagements clarified the regulatory and policy basis of the directive and reaffirmed the government’s position that workers must not be made worse off under the new arrangements. Minerals Commission tasked to protect workers’ conditions To enforce the safeguards, the government has directed the Minerals Commission to ensure that no worker engaged, or to be engaged, by a mining contractor or similar service provider suffers any deterioration or reduction in wages, emoluments, entitlements, benefits or conditions of service because of the transition. The Commission has also been instructed to take steps to harmonise salaries, wages and conditions of service across the mining industry value chain. Another measure requires eligible contractors to be categorised according to their capacity to provide mining-related services. The Ministry said the measures supplemented existing regulatory requirements and did not preclude further lawful action by the Minerals Commission to advance the objectives of the Minerals and Mining (Local Content and Local Participation) Regulations, 2020 (LI 2431). The Commission is expected to complete the processes required to implement the measures and submit the necessary documents for approval by November 30, 2026. Ghanaian companies to lead contract mining The government also reaffirmed the local content requirements governing contract mining in Ghana. Under the policy, indigenous Ghanaian companies are to undertake contract mining for surface mining operations. Underground contract mining must be undertaken through partnerships in which Ghanaian-owned companies hold at least a 50 per cent interest. The requirement was incorporated into the sixth edition of the Local Procurement List, which took effect on January 1, 2025, pursuant to LI 2431. The Ministry said most multinational mining companies operating in Ghana had successfully transitioned their operations to comply with the requirement. It described the experience as evidence that the local content requirement was practicable and enjoyed broad industry support. However, it acknowledged that the transition had raised concerns about the possible implications for workers’ pay and conditions of service, prompting further consultations and the introduction of additional safeguards. Government warns against labour abuses The Ministry said the government would not tolerate practices that undermine local content objectives or disadvantage Ghanaian workers. It specifically warned against unfair labour practices, cartelisation, bid rigging, fronting and other conduct that could undermine genuine Ghanaian participation in the mining industry. Under President John Dramani Mahama’s Reset Agenda, the government said it remained committed to fairness, transparency, genuine Ghanaian participation and the protection of workers across the mining industry value chain. The Ministry said the additional measures were intended to ensure that the implementation of the contract mining policy promoted local participation while safeguarding the rights, remuneration and welfare of mineworkers.

Tinubu meets with Zenith Bank founder Jim Ovia, Budget Office DG in Aso Villa
items.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA– PRESIDENT Bola Tinubu met on Tuesday with Jim Ovia, founder of Zenith Bank and chairman of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) at the Presidential Villa, Abuja. The President also met separately with the Director-General of the Budget Office of the Federation Tanimu Kurfi. Although no official reasons were given for the purposes of both meetings, Ovia arrived at the State House at about 2:15 p.m., dressed in his customary black suit and red tie. It was gathered that the Budget Office chief was on a regular briefing with the President and met him behind closed-doors. The Zenith Bank founder has chaired the NELFUND board since his appointment by President Tinubu on April 26, 2024. Ovia’s appointment came less than three weeks after President Tinubu signed into law the Access to Higher Education Act (Repeal and Re-Enactment) Act, which created the interest-free student-loan scheme. NELFUND provides an interest-free loan to eligible Nigerian tertiary and vocational students to cover approved educational costs. It is voluntary, applied for online, and repaid after graduation and employment through a capped income deduction. items.title: Dangote acquires 25% stake in Kenya pipeline
items.description: Africa’s richest man, Aliko Dangote, says his company has acquired a 25 per cent stake in Kenya Pipeline Company in a deal valued at approximately $327 million. Dangote announced the acquisition on Wednesday at the Financial Times Africa Summit in London, according to Reuters, saying the investment would facilitate the distribution of petroleum products. “We bought 25 per cent of their pipeline network for the distribution of petroleum products,” the president of Dangote Industries Limited said. The acquisition comes as Dangote expands his investments in Africa’s energy sector, including a proposed $16 billion refinery in Kenya designed to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day. On September 30, Dangote and Kenyan President William Ruto broke ground on the proposed refinery at Lamu Port. Dangote said the project would be commissioned within 40 months, adding that it would have a processing capacity comparable to his Nigerian refinery. “We will come back here and commission this refinery in 40 months from today. The East African refinery is designed to process approximately 700,000 barrels of crude per day. It will also generate 1,000 megawatts, twice that of Lagos,” he said. He added that the facility would produce one million tonnes of polypropylene and base oil, as well as supply at least 20 per cent of the jet fuel consumed in Europe and the United Kingdom. The pipeline acquisition follows Ruto’s announcement on Tuesday that private investors had acquired a 25 per cent stake in Kenya’s pipeline network from public entities. The Kenyan president did not identify the investors at the time. Earlier this year, Kenya sold a 65 per cent stake in Kenya Pipeline Company through an initial public offering, in a major privatisation move aimed at raising government revenue amid limited fiscal space. The transaction marked the country’s first major share sale in two decades. The post Dangote acquires 25% stake in Kenya pipeline appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Espèces invasives: quand la Nature attaque la Nature
items.description: Les espèces invasives sont un danger majeur pour la biodiversité. Elles sont responsables de 60% des disparitions d'espèces recensées. Ce sont des animaux ou des plantes amenées par l'Humain dans un milieu qui leur est étranger et dans lequel elles vont pouvoir s'adapter. En devenant des prédateurs d'espèces autochtones, en entrant en concurrence pour les ressources alimentaires ou en se reproduisant avec des espèces locales, ces nouveaux venus vont déséquilibrer les écosystèmes.

items.title: Le Niger sur Kalangou du 21 octobre 2026
items.description: Listen to « Securite alimentaire, preservation de l'environnement et patrimoine culturel (Le Niger sur Kalangou) » on Spreaker. Au menu de l'emission de ce mercredi : Dans l'entretien du jour, nous abordons le droit a l'alimentation au Niger a l'occasion de la journee mondiale de l'alimentation celebree le 16 octobre sous le theme « Innover aujourd'hui pour nourrir demain ». Dans la rubrique Environnement, direction Kablewa, dans la region de Diffa. Plusieurs especes d'arbres ont ete plantees par des jeunes dans le cadre de l'initiative « Kablewa Vert ». Cependant, selon le service communal de l'environnement, une grande partie de ces plantations deperit faute d'entretien et de suivi. Le sergent Moutari Ibrahim, chef du service communal de l'environnement et de la lutte contre la desertification, apporte des explications au micro d'Abdoulaye Maïna. L'echo des regions nous conduit a Dogondoutchi, dans la region de Dosso, pour rendre hommage a Mahamadou Bado, dit Maidawa, decede le dimanche 18 octobre 2026 a l'âge de 72 ans. Principal acteur du ballet Mahalba, qui avait remporte le premier prix au Festival de la jeunesse en 1980, il a continue a participer a des activites culturelles locales. Boubacar Yari, auteur-compositeur du ballet, revient sur son parcours au micro d'Abdoul Aziz Dayouma.
