items.description: Centuries before bookstores had shelves labeled ROMANCE and fictional hockey players locked eyes across the ice, the love story, with all of its attendant joys and sorrows, was an organizing principle of life—and of literature. The sentiment that another person might “complete” us enchanted both Plato and Jerry Maguire, and the search for that someone, along with the desire to understand why it can hurt so bad, has animated fiction from the beginning. The list below is an effort to name those love stories: novels, of course, but also poetry, plays, and short stories—that we consider to be the most enduring. We asked a jury of scholars, librarians, critics, and authors across genres, as well as many colleagues, to name their favorite titles that were originally written in English. We thought of our own personal touchstones, deliberated over the choices, and emerged with a group of standouts: 50 titles you won’t soon forget. English is not reputed to be the most romantic language, but it is the most widely spoken. (Focusing on these particular love stories was also a practical way to narrow things down.) Since the end of the Renaissance, when modern English began to take shape, poets and playwrights wrote tales of wooing and marriage, infatuation and betrayal. Their words gave rise to some of our language’s most powerful aphorisms, idioms, and, yes, clichés—think of hearts on sleeves and matches made in heaven. Today, fictional love is associated with the romance genre and its proliferating subcategories, and you’ll find examples of those books here, but we aimed to think more expansively about its literary manifestations. The love story belongs as much to Arundhati Roy as to Jane Austen; its pulse beats as strongly in the knotty poetry of Anne Carson as it does in the steamy historicals of Beverly Jenkins. It is by turns ecstatic, tragic, cerebral, enthralling, and enlightening. For so many of us, it’s a reason to live and to read. Explore the unforgettable love stories Astrophil and Stella by Philip Sidney 1591 Well before the novel existed to plot out the course of infatuation and heartbreak, grand sequences of sonnets chronicled the rise and fall of great loves. One of the most radical of these was Sidney’s, which follows Astrophil (“star lover” in Greek) and his beloved, the celestial Stella, across 108 sonnets and a handful of songs. To woo her, Astrophil displays his wit via the wordplay that poets have long used to capture the messy states of the heart—and show off the dexterity of the writer. But Sidney’s sequence stands out because of his awareness that the formal devices peppered across his poems are “stol’n goods.” And he wrote a truly compelling story, one that keeps us in suspense until the middle of the series, when Astrophil’s eyes meet Stella’s. Although his paradoxical blandishments may not win him his star in the end, they are a triumph in their own right, seducing and amusing us in a portrait of love-tossed misery. Walt Hunter Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare 1597 Shakespeare’s tragedy about young lovers from rival families remains, four centuries later, one of the most adapted plays in the English language. In just the past 30 years, Leonardo DiCaprio, Jet Li, Aaliyah, and Angelina Jolie have all played versions of Romeo or Juliet. There’s been a zombie version and several Bollywood ones. The play was even, if you’ll believe it, reinterpreted with gnomes. (His name becomes Gnomeo, obviously.) The story is inescapable but persists, I think, because of its tantalizing core premise: that you could find a love so passionate, so all-consuming, that you’d rather die than be without it. Serena Dai Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister by Aphra Behn 1684 Behn, best known for her plays and her later novel Oroonoko , was the rare woman to make a living as a writer in the 17th century. This epistolary saga endures, in part, because of its salaciousness. The passion between the aptly named Philander and Silvia, his wife’s sister, is absolutely cursed; their most significant shared interest appears to be bringing upheaval and misery into the lives of everyone they meet. Although the central affair may be unenviable, the book is notable for the sheer range of romantic literary tropes that it helped enshrine—including the wayward lover who only wants what he can’t have, the once-pure soul corrupted by sexual liberty, and the fake relationship that gives rise to real feelings. Above all, it proves that swooning language, nonstop drama, and a tinge of the illicit can make a romance an addictive read, even (and sometimes especially) when its characters are offputting. Talya Zax Evelina by Frances Burney 1778 Burney’s novel is a romance in every sense of the word. Yes, it’s a book about the golden-hearted young woman of the title, Evelina, falling in love with a wealthy, dashing young man—a preview of the marriage plots of Jane Austen, who counted Burney as one of her favorite authors. But it’s also a romantic novel in the older literary sense, the kind of mildly fantastical tale in which an impoverished Scottish poet considers turning to a life of crime, only to wed an heiress once it becomes apparent that she is not, as was previously suspected, his half sister. Evelina’s blissfully unrealistic quest for both love and personal recognition—spoiler: she turns out to be an heiress too—is both sharply observant and a lark. It deserves more love from a literary culture that adores Austen but often ignores her predecessors. Talya Zax Persuasion by Jane Austen 1817 Austen is the empress of romance, and her work sets the bar for all of the love stories patterned after hers. Pride and Prejudice , Sense and Sensibility , and Emma each could rightfully claim a spot on this list. But Persuasion is Austen’s most mature and realistic novel. It tells the story of a single, not-so-young woman who is reunited after many years with the man she rejected at 19. Its prose is calmer and less intent on cleverness than Austen’s other works, and it is suffused with the disappointments and hardships that accompany any life lived past the age of 20. So the happy ending, when it inevitably comes—this is still a classic romance, after all—feels especially well-earned. Eleanor Barkhorn Jane Eyre by Charlotte Brontë 1847 The full title of this coming-of-age novel is Jane Eyre: An Autobiography . That deliberate move emphasizes the authority of the titular heroine—a governess who is poor, orphaned, and unbeautiful—to narrate the story of her life. So it is impossible to discuss the soul-cracking love story between Jane and her employer, Edward Rochester of Thornfield Hall, without paying heed to Jane’s assertion of control when she learns, to her horror, that Rochester is already married to a Creole woman named Bertha Mason. Bertha is treated cruelly by both Rochester and the author, and Jane ultimately profits from her suffering. Whether one blames Jane is another topic. But this famous book’s famous line toward the end—“Reader, I married him”—states her case: Jane’s allegiance is not the passive sort. She owns her decision. Rachel Vorona Cote Wuthering Heights by Emily Brontë 1847 Few, if any, books on this list should be read as a how-to guide for the romantically inclined. That said, you really, really, really shouldn’t model your affairs on the doomed relationship that propels Brontë’s only novel. Wuthering Heights conjures a vision of love as despair and longing, not a living thing to be nurtured but a cold, hard object clutched fervently to your chest. When Victorian-era social mores keep the childhood sweethearts Cathy and Heathcliff apart, Heathcliff decides that nobody in their vicinity should ever be happy, and drafts a revenge plot to upend an already-miserable family. Also, everyone is constantly dying of consumption or trying to kill a dog. Nonetheless, this is the stuff of messy myth, the sort of lifelong obsession that makes all other entanglements seem paltry and cheap. Naturally, the pair is reunited only in death, as their specters meet again on the windswept moorlands. Jeremy Gordon North and South by Elizabeth Gaskell 1854 With the rise of industry in mid-19th-century England came the industrial novel, an improbably romantic genre. In Gaskell’s version, a rocky courtship mirrors the country’s labor wars. The cultured, genteel Margaret Hale is forced to leave a village in the agrarian south for a squalid city in the industrial north (a thinly disguised Manchester), where she gets caught up in the lives of desperately poor workers. Meanwhile, she is befriended by a Byronic, self-made cotton-mill owner, John Thornton. The novel tracks her sentimental education—and his—as they overcome class prejudices and hotly debate Thornton’s obligations to his employees. A strike and near riot lead to a shocking, at least by the standards of the day, public display of affection; the greater the threat of violence becomes, the more the book swoons. Imagine Pride and Prejudice updated for a more political age, and you’ll get a sense of the pleasures of North and South . Judith Shulevitz Middlemarch by George Eliot 1871 Eliot wrote novels about marriages both good and bad, usually bad. In Middlemarch , these unions function as worlds unto themselves—created by, but larger than, the couples inside of them—and the bad ones crush the soul. Two of this novel’s several protagonists, Dorothea Brooke and Tertius Lydgate, suffer from romantic illusions, and each chooses an utterly unsuitable partner: The idealistic Dorothea thinks she’s marrying a great scholar, but he turns out to be spectacularly mediocre, so tyrannical and small-minded that his last name, Casaubon, has become shorthand for “pettifogging pedant.” Lydgate has a brilliant future as a doctor but falls for a beautiful, vain woman with expensive social aspirations. One of these two will be trapped for life, and the other freed only by an act of God. Eliot is willing to give characters a chance at love, though, and the horribleness of the bad marriages makes the good ones feel like a major spiritual achievement. Judith Shulevitz The Portrait of a Lady by Henry James 1881 Should The Portrait of a Lady be considered one of James’s ghost stories? The characters are alive but their choices linger like a haunting, and when I think of this classic, I feel as though I’m encountering a phantom. The story of Isabel Archer, a young woman who wants to believe that her life is her own to determine, is classic James, down to its settings and psychological contradictions. The friends Isabel encounters are taken with who she is and ache to see her get what she wants, just as the reader will; the men and women who want to use her for their own needs are villains unlike any other—their machinations are what haunt me. This is all to say it’s the most romantic book I’ve ever read, one that understands how dangerous it is to be a woman who believes in love’s powers—and yet how necessary it is to retain that belief, no matter the fears that hang over us. Haley Mlotek Anne of the Island by L. M. Montgomery 1915 When readers meet Anne Shirley, she’s an irresistible mess of contradictions: an 11-year-old tomboy who’s vain about her looks, an occasional liar who is also capable of searching honesty. These qualities make her unforgettable to those around her, not least to Gilbert Blythe, the boy in class who teases her, competes with her, befriends her, and ultimately becomes her lifelong love. The joy of the Anne of Green Gables series lies in the specific delights of watching Anne grow up—and in how affectionately it widens its lens to show us Gilbert growing up next to her. Anne of the Island , the third book, is where this happens in earnest, as the two head to college and wrestle with what they want from the wider world. As almost-adults, Anne and Gilbert look for love with other people, get jobs as teachers, and learn about sacrifice and (on one particular night) the possibility of loss. The twists and turns are classic, but you’ll thrill at seeing both of them wend their way toward the other, because you know how lively a partnership theirs will be: These two friends, who know each other better than anyone else, are idiosyncratic as individuals and will be no less so as a couple. Jane Yong Kim The Age of Innocence by Edith Wharton 1920 Wharton’s magnum opus is a voyeur’s novel, written for those who love to gawk, by a woman who invited her readers to gape at New York’s “small and slippery pyramid” of Gilded Age high society. Among its velvet-caped, silver-spooned denizens, someone is always, always watching. The Age of Innocence is an agonizing tale of the rigors of unconsummated love. The dutiful Newland Archer is blissfully engaged to the demure May Welland until he spies her cousin, Ellen Olenska—who has just returned from a broken, ruinous marriage—at the opera. Ellen is everything Newland craves: cultured, candid, independent. She’s simultaneously drawn to him and hobbled by guilt. But being together would mean betraying May. So how will they exist—and coexist—in stifling, closely surveilled Manhattan? The novel’s last image, a gaze at a closing window, is as heartbreaking as any of literature’s most dramatic deaths. Hillary Kelly The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald 1925 I know, I know: The Great Gatsby is a love story in the way that Jaws is a nature documentary. But the romance between Jay Gatsby and Daisy Buchanan—slow-burning, explosive, doomed—endures precisely because it is so richly unromantic. This affair, as it picks up speed, threatens everyone in its path. Gatsby pines for Daisy and waits for Daisy and reinvents himself for Daisy. He builds, and then takes residence in, a Daisy-centric universe. In another novel, that kind of devotion would be something to be celebrated—desire as a physical force, passion as the ultimate plot device. In Fitzgerald’s masterpiece, though, passion is also an omen; like Chekhov’s gun, or George Wilson’s, it is always lying in wait. But the novel, having stripped romance of its giddiness, offers something far more compelling in return: ambivalence. Is this devotion? Is it delusion? Or is it one more party, glittering and wild, that will have to come to an end? Megan Garber The Bridge of San Luis Rey by Thornton Wilder 1927 When a rope bridge in Peru collapses in July 1714, killing five people, the Franciscan friar Brother Juniper wants to know: Why did these five souls perish—was it an accident or divine intention? This simple question propels Wilder’s Pulitzer Prize–winning novel into a brilliant exploration of attachment and its flawed, human expressions—the suffocating love of the Marquesa for her daughter; the self-sacrificing love of young Pepita for the abbess who raised her; the codependent love between the twin brothers Esteban and Manuel, which leaves no room for romance; and the manipulative love of Uncle Pio for the great actor La Perichole. Almost 100 years after The Bridge of San Luis Rey was first published, its last sentence still feels like a surprise ending, somehow striking a hopeful note: “There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning.” Molly Roden Winter Their Eyes Were Watching God by Zora Neale Hurston 1937 Janie Crawford is a freethinking Black woman who yearns for a steady love, but her quest for it ultimately leads her toward her own highest self. Marriage, in this novel, can be disfiguring, and it forces women to shrink parts of themselves. Before she’s 40, Janie has been through two painful relationships with men who harm her, belittle her, and control her. But even when she’s curled in on herself, Hurston’s microscopic gaze manages to show us the fine grooves of Janie’s heart. Finally, approaching middle age, she meets and marries a younger man named Tea Cake; her feelings for him are so intense that she experiences a “self-crushing love.” But the line that shook me is as follows: “So her soul crawled out from its hiding place.” She genuinely adores Tea Cake, but their marriage, too, will end—and, wisely, she’ll have saved an ounce more of that love for herself. Jenisha Watts Arabella by Georgette Heyer 1949 Arabella is the blueprint for modern Regency romances—the whole etiquette-driven Bridgerton -esque subgenre. The title character is the eldest daughter of a poor country vicar, and she must marry well for the sake of her younger siblings. Mr. Beaumaris is the richest, most eligible local bachelor—and he’s committed to staying single and away from scheming women. To save her pride, Arabella tells Mr. Beaumaris a string of lies. Amused and intrigued, he stays in her endearing orbit, content to watch her navigate the ridiculous situations these lies get her into, until they both fall madly for each other. Hilarious and deeply romantic, the 1949 novel offers historical detail and sharp commentary on the era’s social conventions that make it feel as if Heyer was writing alongside Jane Austen in 1817. Danica Nava The End of the Affair by Graham Greene 1951 The End of the Affair is the fourth and final of Greene’s “Catholic novels.” The book’s autofictional protagonist, Maurice Bendrix, has a passionate affair with the married Sarah Miles. Their union is plagued by his jealousy; after Bendrix’s London apartment is bombed during World War II, Sarah ends things abruptly. A private investigator reveals that Sarah had promised God that she would quit the affair if Bendrix survived. More drama ensues, but the book’s real accomplishment is its close examination of the nature of ardor. I first read it at 19, and although I am not a Catholic, I was raised by one, and I inherited something of his tormented relationship to devotion. The question the book left me with was one that I had wondered before, if cautiously: What if all love derives, ultimately, from the divine? Melissa Febos The Price of Salt by Patricia Highsmith 1952 When Highsmith’s 1952 novel opens, the 19-year-old Therese Belivet is working the Christmas rush at a Manhattan department store. With its crowded workers’ canteen and lonely employees, the store is likened to a prison. One day, a blond woman with a fur coat and gray eyes approaches Therese’s counter, and Highsmith leaves the administered world of the department store for the open road. Compared with Todd Haynes’s ravishing 2015 film adaptation, Carol , the novel is spikier, more political, and attentive to the repression and surveillance of Cold War America. Highsmith’s eye for quotidian detail gives the writing a lived-in quality: When, two-thirds of the way through, the two women share their first kiss, Therese notices the lock of hair toppling over Carol’s scarf, the scratch on the toe of her moccasin. Their devotion is ordinary, anchored in everyday things—but it is this kind of love, the book suggests, that might set us free. Charlie Tyson Giovanni’s Room by James Baldwin 1956 Giovanni’s Room is a novel of terrible romantic abjection. David, an idle American in Paris, frightened and ashamed of his attraction to men, meets Giovanni, an Italian who has fled his country and works at a gay bar. Their love is, from the beginning, doomed by David’s unremitting self-hatred—his imprisonment in his own “dirty body” and his fear of its uncontrollable, irresistible longings. Desire is always shadowed by disgust, which casts a tragic pall over these two lovers in the city of lights. Merve Emre Maurice by E. M. Forster 1971 In 1913, Forster had a life-changing experience: A man touched his “backside—gently and just above the buttocks,” as he described it later. Forster was 34 years old and already established as one of England’s best novelists, but he had never come to terms with his homosexuality, much less written about it. Now he set to work on a love story about two men. What made Maurice revolutionary was Forster’s insistence that Maurice Hall, the repressed, middle-class protagonist, not meet with a tragic ending—the usual fate of gay characters in fiction at the time. Instead, he and Alec Scudder, a working-class gamekeeper, fall in love and, as Alec declares, decide that they “shan’t be parted no more, and that’s finished.” Even after completing the novel, Forster felt it was too radical to publish. When it finally appeared in 1971, after his death, Maurice already seemed a little old-fashioned to critics. But even today, there is great power in the novel’s undefended emotion—the tremulous happiness of a wish fulfilled. Adam Kirsch The Flame and the Flower by Kathleen E. Woodiwiss 1972 This is the godmother of all bodice rippers. As might be expected of a ’70s novel set in antebellum Charleston, South Carolina, the modern reader may want a heads up: It includes sexual assault, slavery, and kidnapping—but contemporary objections can’t override its compelling central pairing. Heather Simmons, an innocent British orphan, and Brandon Birmingham, a stubborn American ship captain, overcome their harrowing first encounter and cultural differences to give themselves permission to love. Heather learns to take control of her life, and Brandon promises to spend the rest of his making up for any pain she’s suffered. Explicit sex scenes, rare in books of the time, reveal the intimacy usually elided by “fade to black” paragraphs, and their influence can still be found today in heaps of romantic subgenres. Woodiwiss’s detailed, lush prose inspires both wistful admiration and, however begrudging, real respect. Nichole Perkins Corregidora by Gayl Jones 1975 Has Ursa Corregidora ever really been loved? She was a deeply wanted daughter, yes—in part so she could fill the role of a Corregidora woman. From a young age, she has known that her job is to remember the violence done to their family during slavery and to “make generations” that will pass down that memory. Her husband, Mutt, courted her, praised her, and bedded her—then he threw her down the stairs, leading to an emergency hysterectomy that left her childless. Men and women constantly paw at her, demanding affection, fidelity, and sex. So Ursa has a hard shell, and she knows how to hate. She’s scared, though, that she doesn’t know what love looks like. In the course of this short, bleak, transportive book, no one will sweep her off her feet to show her. But she’ll be able to recognize what it’s not: “You can’t kiss where you scratched anymore,” she resolves. “You don’t treat love that way.” Emma Sarappo Endless Love by Scott Spencer 1979 After 45 years, I can still recite this novel’s intense opening lines. I wasn’t 17, as the narrator is—I read the novel during my junior year of college—but I wanted to be, like him, in full obedience to my heart’s most urgent commands. This is the kind of book that, if you allow it, will seize you from the first and never let you go, then consume your imagination long after you finish. Endless Love is an unashamed dive into the monomania of romantic obsession. It contains one of the most honest, longest, bloodiest sex scenes in all of literature. It also conveys the pain and sadness of being that young, wanting that much, and running up hard against the limits of your world and your self. I haven’t read Endless Love since I was 20. Today I might find it marred by its excesses, but that might be a sign of something lacking in myself. George Packer The Transit of Venus by Shirley Hazzard 1980 Midway through The Transit of Venus , the awkward, brilliant scientist Ted Tice learns that Caroline Bell—the object of his unrequited passion and the heroine of the novel—has married. In his subsequent daze, he finds that “grief had a painter’s eye, assigning arbitrary meaning at random—like God.” Has personal tragedy ever sounded more enthralling? Hazzard’s masterpiece follows the orphaned Caroline and her sister, Grace, through the decades of profound change that followed World War II, as each discovers how love can circumscribe a life. Few of the relationships in this novel are happy, but all of them are so finely wrought that to read them is almost to live them—to feel, as Ted does, with an intensity that is both painful and enlightening. Talya Zax Love Medicine by Louise Erdrich 1984 The titular potion in Love Medicine does not work as planned. In fact, the overriding theme of Erdrich’s debut novel, a prismatic saga following one Chippewa family, is that love can be neither predicted nor controlled. The Kashpaws form a giant tumbleweed of a family tree, whose complexity owes to a love triangle in the early 20th century. The progenitors are the handsome, passive Nector; his headstrong wife, Marie; and the wandering Lulu, who goes on to have a brood of children with different fathers. Erdrich’s panorama makes room for dozens of fascinating characters, but the love story sets everything in motion, and decades later it comes to a perfectly fitting conclusion. Love Medicine is, among many things, a brief against shame. As Lulu says when she gets to plead her case, “When they tell you that I was heartless, a shameless man-chaser, don’t ever forget this: I loved what I saw.” Boris Kachka Beloved by Toni Morrison 1987 Beloved asks readers to imagine something as pure and perfect as love—a mother caring for her child; two broken people trying to make something beautiful—in the face of absolute misery and ugliness. That’s where the book’s potency comes from: the tension between the darkness and the light. Sethe, its main character, has committed unspeakable violence toward her own daughter, but she was motivated by maternal devotion. Having survived that transformational tragedy, she has to decide whether she can allow anyone to love her again. Beloved evokes both the peril of motherhood and its singular power. Reading it, I wanted to fold myself into the pages and then fall out of my skin. It’s painful, but what’s even more devastating is that the novel is one of the most banned books in America. How dare we rob the next generation of its greatness? Jenisha Watts The Remains of the Day by Kazuo Ishiguro 1989 This novel is, to borrow a term from Saint Augustine, a story of disordered love. Stevens, the narrator, is an impeccably mannered British butler who loves his country, his profession, and his master—all worthy enough objects of devotion, in the abstract. His fidelity blinds him, however, to the cruelty and fecklessness that his nation and employer are capable of—and to just how humiliating some of his work can be. Even more tragically, his sense of duty compels him to deny love to the flesh-and-blood humans in his midst: He abandons his dying father so that he can better tend to a dinner his master is hosting; he refuses to acknowledge, let alone reciprocate, the clear affection of a fellow servant. The anguish of reading this novel lies in watching a man with such a deep capacity for love direct it to exactly the wrong places. Eleanor Barkhorn Possession by A. S. Byatt 1990 Possession opens in 1986, in the reading room of the London Library, where mysterious letters discovered by a young academic jolt the plot into action. It ends in the 19th century, with a devastating scene in which the letters’ author stops to chat with a child. In between is a detective story about two sets of prospective lovers more than 100 years apart: In the 1980s, a dueling pair of scholars—one the careful, if old-fashioned, philologist who finds the letters and the other a glamorous, feminist critic—seek to understand a secret romance through notes and correspondence. In the past, we meet the Victorian poets who are the subjects of that search as they leave behind the traces that will be puzzled over and plumbed. The book is extravagant, high-concept, and a total tearjerker, distinctive for its empathy toward its characters and their sense of the possible—and for its many passages of people falling head over heels for each other’s writing. Hillary Chute Mating by Norman Rush 1991 “Why do we yield” to love, asks this novel’s narrator, “when we don’t have to?” She’s an intellectually voracious anthropologist overwhelmed by a new romance—and she’d “like to know as a woman and a human being, both.” Mating is Rush’s effort to get to the bottom of that unanswerable question: Why is it that sex and love make the smartest, most confident, and most in-control of us fall apart? But the novel isn’t just intellectual; far from it. Rush gives his book every possible kind of drama, from the erotic to the geopolitical—and, what’s more, he imbues his writing with a real (if wry) optimism that has turned Mating into a cult classic of our sometimes-pessimistic age. Lily Meyer The Blue Flower by Penelope Fitzgerald 1995 When the German Romantic poet Novalis, real name Friedrich “Fritz” von Hardenburg, was in his early 20s, he fell in love with a 12-year-old named Sophie von Kühn. (This utterly inappropriate match was thankfully never consummated, owing to her early death.) In his grief, Novalis wrote a fragmentary novel about a man who longs to see a mysterious “blue flower,” which would provide the material for Fitzgerald’s gently comic, subtly insightful book. Here, Fritz’s idolization of the distinctly ordinary Sophie, whom he calls “my wisdom” and “my Philosophy,” is clearly the ridiculous acting-out of a young man who wants drama—but in Fitzgerald’s skillful hands, it’s also an idealistic, even beautiful, pursuit of the self-abnegation that can come with love. Lily Meyer “Brokeback Mountain” by Annie Proulx 1997 The source material for the film that won Ang Lee an Oscar and became pop-culture shorthand is only about 10,000 words long. How, in just one short story, did Proulx manage to fit in one of the most stirring depictions of romantic ecstasy that I’ve ever read? Her measured, inventive sentences follow Jack and Ennis, who meet in the summer of 1963 while herding sheep on Brokeback Mountain, in Wyoming, and experience a lightning-strike intimacy that keeps them tied together for decades. Proulx wrote what became the film’s most memorable line—“I wish I knew how to quit you”—but much of the story’s prose should be equally famous. Chronology is dictated here only by desire—years go by in a paragraph; a single embrace oozes across a page. Love, Proulx shows, warps the minutes: Every meeting both lasts forever and ends in an agonizing second. Valerie Trapp The God of Small Things by Arundhati Roy 1997 In her Booker Prize – winning novel about the tragic fallout of a taboo-breaking liaison, Roy repeats a few distinct phrases again and again. One is the image of a “hole in the Universe” that takes various shapes: a person, or a cat, or “History.” Although The God of Small Things overflows with monsoon-drenched flora, industrial pollutants, bitterness, and scheming, it has a love-shaped hole in its center that is filled only at the very end. From the first pages, we know that Estha and Rahel, fraternal twins in a prosperous but dissipated family in India’s Kerala region, have seen their lives ruined after a blurry sequence of events that led to death and exile. Slowly, inevitably, Roy closes in on a brief, forbidden dalliance that defies India’s caste system. Romance, in this story, is usually defined by its absence, and yet passion is everywhere. Sometimes desire blooms beautifully; more often, it remains untended, left to rot. Boris Kachka I Love Dick by Chris Kraus 1997 When this book was first published, the Dick of the title, a real-life sociologist, was quoted in New York magazine denigrating the work as “a bad review of my presence in the world.” This revealed his identity, even though Kraus had tried partly to obscure it—after all, the book isn’t a memoir. It’s instead a species of autofiction, a collection of billets-doux to Dick written by Kraus’s protagonist, also named Chris, with her husband, named Sylvère, like Kraus’s actual then-husband. Her aim is to “take an experience that was so completely female”—the private, abject state of unrequited romantic obsession—and treat it seriously, like material for academic study. What results is a genre-bending feminist work powered by the engine of infatuation. As Chris puts it: “Desire isn’t lack, it’s surplus energy.” Dick is right that he doesn’t come out looking so great, but the book is only nominally about him anyway. Christina McCausland Tipping the Velvet by Sarah Waters 1998 Waters’s moving portrait of the anguish that follows falling in and out of love is as erotic as it is engrossing. After a young girl named Nan becomes smitten with Kitty, a “masher” (or male impersonator), she follows her new flame to London, only to endure a terrible betrayal. The Victorian capital has never been as alive as it is in Tipping the Velvet : The 19th-century theater world gives way to the city’s seedy underground before the book peeks in on socialist organizing. Every plot thread is loaded with commentary on class, sexuality, and gender. Beautiful, passionate, and historically clever, this is no ordinary bildungsroman. Chinelo Okparanta Autobiography of Red by Anne Carson 1998 A little red monster with wings falls in love with the Greek hero Herakles. The two go to hell to visit Herakles’s grandmother, break up, and reunite years later at a Peruvian volcano. Autobiography of Red claims to have recovered this improbable plot from bits of writing by Stesichoros, a Greek poet from the sixth century B.C.E.; Carson begins with invented “fragments” from Stesichoros and three scholarly looking appendixes before starting her original, woozy love story in earnest. Early on, Geryon is 14, abused by his brother and adored by his mother. A chance encounter with Herakles at a bus station leads to a teenage romance and some of the most transcendent love poetry of the late 20th century. Geryon ultimately finds his calling as a photographer; the book concludes with a description of his snapshots, which arrest the characters in a state of longing—with “immortality on their faces, night at their back.” Walt Hunter Peel My Love Like an Onion by Ana Castillo 1999 Flamenco isn’t just a dance for Carmen Santos, she reminds us frequently. It’s a way of life. It gave her the ability to walk without crutches when she was a child, her leg withered by polio; it gave her a living in her 20s; it allowed her to make art when no one believed that she could. And it introduced her to the two great loves of her life: her older mentor, Agustín, who brought her into his company and made her his mistress for 17 years, and the young dancer Manolo, who gave her a year of passion unlike any she’d known before. Now Carmen is approaching 40, living at home in Chicago, and unable to dance—post-polio syndrome is taking away her hard-earned dexterity. Her mother wishes she’d married and had children, but Carmen regrets nothing. And when both Agustín and Manolo come back into her life, she won’t pretend that her heart is closed—but she knows there are things she won’t give up for love. Emma Sarappo Atonement by Ian McEwan 2001 In one sense, Atonement is a classic love story: a sweeping, romantic account of two people pulled to each other with inexplicable, magnetic force. Yet few interactions between Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis actually occur in these pages; their relationship is a specter, mostly present in the hovering question of what could have been. Early on, Briony—a precocious 13-year-old writer—walks in on Cecilia, her older sister, having sex with Robbie, their housekeeper’s son. Misunderstanding what she’s seen, or perhaps motivated to puppet-master reality as she does in her stories, Briony makes a false accusation that lands Robbie in prison. The rest of the book is about her decision’s ruinous repercussions. Some novels cast love as a type of fiction, a comforting yarn spun by humans who can never really access one another’s internal worlds. In Atonement , love is a fact—and the cruelest thing that a story can do is endanger it. Faith Hill Call Me by Your Name by André Aciman 2007 Readers familiar only with the film might be surprised by the elegance and interiority of Aciman’s writing. No author since Proust has given readers such a nuanced understanding of the human heart—not just the forward arrow of reciprocated desire but also the insecurities, crossed signals, ambiguity, and doubt. Call Me By Your Name is a novel that, at last, tells the truth about love. Andrew Sean Greer The Song of Achilles by Madeline Miller 2011 Almost 15 years after The Song of Achilles was first published, the bookstore I co-own, the Ripped Bodice, still sells dozens of copies every month. Few other books have this kind of staying power. Miller’s lyrical retelling of The Iliad , focused on Patroclus and Achilles’s romance, is tender, intimate, achingly sentimental, and—because readers know from the beginning where their story is headed—completely devastating. This is one of those rare stories that seems to become more beloved with every passing year. Leah Koch The Marriage Plot by Jeffrey Eugenides 2011 Eugenides’s love triangle between three brilliant but naive recent college graduates captures the angst and tumult of having one’s ideals tested by disappointment. His characters exit school steeped in 19th-century novels, semiotics, and the academic-seminar trends of the 1980s, which give grammar and form to their fizzing fantasies but also set them up for hard lessons when they inevitably crash into reality. As both a fan of Eugenides and a recovering English major, I ate this up when it came out, in 2011, and revisit it every couple of years out of affectionate nostalgia. Jon Hickey Americanah by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie 2013 Ifemelu, a feisty, fiercely intelligent fellow at Princeton and a prolific blogger, is considering returning home, to Lagos, after living in America for many years. Her story is juxtaposed with that of her high-school sweetheart, Obinze, who is now married and a successful businessman. They had lost touch in their youth, when Ifemelu migrated to America and Obinze headed to London—but as the book fills us in on their formative years as a teenage couple and the diverging paths that followed, circumstances lead them back to Nigeria and back to each other. In the past, Adichie has objected to the book being classified as a love story , but even she admits that in the end, it is. I agree: Not only is this a love story; it’s an epic one. Nicole Dennis-Benn Fates and Furies by Lauren Groff 2015 The best love stories suggest something about how all relationships function—even when they imply something dark. Fates and Furies concerns the charming and lucky Lotto and his reserved, mysterious wife, Mathilde. First, we hear Lotto’s account of their life together; it’s a compelling drama, if curiously devoid of details about Mathilde’s background. Then we get Mathilde’s version, which reveals how much Lotto never understood, how willing he was to accept a convenient, two-dimensional idea of his wife. Some of the plot details stretch credulity, resulting in a sort of twisted fable of matrimony. Even then, Groff leaves the reader with the chilling suspicion that every ordinary marriage will end, by death or divorce, with its two partners never having grasped the person they’re meant to know best. Faith Hill Forbidden by Beverly Jenkins 2016 Jenkins is one of the most important voices in modern romance, and Forbidden is a perfect example of what she does best. Set during Reconstruction, the novel follows Black characters building lives, communities, and futures in the aftermath of slavery. Yet the weight of that history never overwhelms Rhine and Eddy’s sharp, funny courtship or the rich world that surrounds them. Jenkins has spent decades showing us that Black history is also a story of joy, ambition, and friendship. Forbidden expands our understanding of who gets to be at the center of the American conversation—and it’s also incredibly fun to read. Leah Koch Normal People by Sally Rooney 2018 Rooney is a master of miscommunication. Her two protagonists here, Marianne and Connell, are as star-crossed as Shakespeare’s doomed lovers, and not only because they, too, come from tragically incompatible homes. The main problem, rather, is that they cannot speak plainly about their desires. A classic example: Connell asks Marianne if she wants to see other people, hoping she’ll say no; she thinks that he’s breaking up with her and coldly replies, “Sure.” Revisiting the book recently, I felt the desperate need to ask them to please use their words. But Normal People is about being young—really young—and navigating feelings that are more powerful than your expressive abilities. I found the novel painfully effective at transporting me back to my teens: a time when everything happens in high definition, someone can feel both made for you and completely inscrutable, and the stakes seem paralyzingly high even when they’re patently low. That’s a bit how falling in love feels at any age. Faith Hill An American Marriage by Tayari Jones 2018 Jones’s breakout fourth novel is set in Atlanta—and, like much of her work, it’s an ode to her hometown. It also has more to say about the contemporary American justice system than almost any other novel written in this century. At the start of the book, Celestial, its artist heroine, is newly, happily married to a striver named Roy, a former small-town boy thrilled to take his place among Atlanta’s Black bourgeoisie. But when Roy is wrongfully arrested and incarcerated, Celestial discovers that even her family wants her to perform a stifling public role as his loyal wife that, no matter how much she loves him, leaves no room for the complexity of her grief and loneliness. When her longtime friendship with her childhood neighbor Andre turns romantic, the position that Roy’s imprisonment has put her in is revealed to be untenable—and Jones reveals Celestial to be a heroine for the ages. Lily Meyer This Is How You Lose the Time War by Amal El-Mohtar and Max Gladstone 2019 In this otherworldly novella, love spans time—and then breaks it. Red and Blue are two futuristic agents embroiled in a war fought across universes and decades; their job is to warp world events in order to benefit their opposing governments. Their correspondence begins with taunts before morphing into mutual curiosity, fascination, and, finally, a passionate and forbidden alliance. Their letters explore yearning with such beauty that I challenge any reader to be unaffected. Red’s and Blue’s very essences are at odds, yet they find each other through battle, through centuries, and through twists in their own timelines that hint of betrayal—but are actually proof of a selfless commitment to a dreamed-of future. El-Mohtar and Gladstone’s deft epistolary romance is, in every sense of the word, timeless. Ashley Herring Blake Before I Let Go by Kennedy Ryan 2022 When we first meet the central couple in Before I Let Go , they are already divorced. A series of tragedies have pushed Yasmen and Josiah apart, and they’re separately navigating grief while still co-parenting and working together. Heartbreak and second chances are familiar territory in romance novels, but Ryan’s novel transcends the commonplace. Her story starts with intense passion and adoration—and then, when the unrelenting stressors and crises of the real world interfere, Ryan asks: Is love alone enough to sustain a marriage? Through Yasmen and Josiah, the reader experiences tender moments of self-doubt and self-loathing, the pride of watching someone build themself up, and the spark of desire reigniting after years of being swept aside. Their reconciliation isn’t wrapped in a perfect bow; it’s messy, mercurial, and imperfect—as Ryan writes, “the stuff real happily ever afters were made of.” Krystle Champagne-Norwood You Made a Fool of Death With Your Beauty by Akwaeke Emezi 2022 Feyi, a Nigerian American artist living in Brooklyn, is dealing with the death of her husband in complicated ways. She pushes for a risky hookup in a bathroom at a party; she paints canvases with animal blood. None of it stops her from having vivid nightmares about how Jonah died—but she’s still trying to move on. She has a not-quite-boyfriend, Nasir, who sweeps her off to his family’s luxurious Caribbean-island estate. Once there, she finds herself drawn to Nasir’s father, Alim, who recognizes Feyi’s sadness. The resulting entanglement is tense, chaotic, and, it must be said, pretty sexy. But the novel isn’t just about the thrill and devastation of an inconvenient attraction. Emezi considers the ways that loss can reshape desire—and the relief that comes from not only being wanted by someone, but also being understood by them. Elise Hannum Little Rabbit by Alyssa Songsiridej 2022 That title is what he calls her—no real names here. He’s “the choreographer,” and she’s just “Rabbit.” They meet in Maine, at an artist’s residency, where nothing happens between them. When they catch up in New York, she’s pulled to him like a dowsing rod to water. She’s queer and hasn’t been with a man in ages. He’s an established artist—rich, powerful, and two decades her senior. At 30, she feels that she knows herself well enough, as a writer and a woman, to indulge her erotic curiosity. Then, before she realizes it, she’s caught in his rip current, being pulled further and further away from everything she knows. The only part that terrifies her: She likes it. Adores it, even. Their partnership remakes everything she’d taken for granted, and Little Rabbit is the story of a person learning to accept what her body’s already decided. Emma Sarappo The Safekeep by Yael van der Wouden 2024 At the beginning of the 1960s, Isabel lives alone in her family home, a house she doesn’t own but has nonetheless burrowed into and absorbed as her whole way of life. One night at dinner, her brother and landlord, Louis, introduces Eva, his girlfriend, who repulses the tightly wound Isabel with her “violently peroxided bob” and overt sexuality. When Louis suggests that Eva move in with Isabel for the summer, Isabel’s furious suspicion turns into erotic obsession. Van der Wouden builds the revelations so elegantly that to spoil them would feel like critical malpractice. The house is more than a house; Isabel’s sour, anxious misanthropy is more than simple repression. And Eva is so much more than a vehicle for sexual awakening—she’s also a puzzle, and she inspires a reckoning. But the ferocious connection between the two women seems to incinerate all of the layers of history and conflict that engulf them, creating space for something new. Sophie Gilbert

items.title: Macron takes aim at Trump for using France riots for election gain
items.description: President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday took an apparent swipe at counterpart Donald Trump of exploiting France’s riots for advantage in the US midterm election battle, as Paris prepared for more protests this weekend. Macron, speaking during a visit to Qatar, implied that Trump, and possibly Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is also in election mode , made “stupid comments” on the unrest for political gain, though he did not name either leader. “There are people who campaign at France’s expense — leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic,” he told reporters in Doha. Macron made his remarks as he and his government struggled to get on top of a crisis that has scarred France’s image both abroad and in financial markets, six months ahead of presidential elections to choose his successor. France’s government has admitted it “lost control” in the frenzy of street violence that erupted last weekend, when masked youths clashed with police, looted shops and vandalised public buildings. Trump has sought to link the “revolution” in France to “migrants, jihadists, and communists” as he campaigned for his Republican party in the United States on his anti-immigration messaging. He also on Tuesday hailed French far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who shares his ideologies, as a conservative voice, with surveys putting her as the frontrunner in France’s presidential race. Trump’s ally Netanyahu, facing his own tough election battle, on Tuesday argued that France had been hit by an “invasion of extremist Islam”. Several analysts have dismissed the claims that migrants were driving France’s protests. Curfews The unrest overshadowed demonstrations held on Saturday in which more than half a million people marched nationwide against the cost of living. Those rallies followed four weeks of student protests that have closed many schools across France. Since the rioting — the worst France has seen in years — and ahead of further cost-of-living demonstrations this coming Saturday, Macron’s government has warned it will brook no further violence. Authorities in Paris and several other cities imposed nighttime curfews Monday and Tuesday in certain zones prone to protests or looting. Macron said that on Thursday he would chair a meeting of key ministers and intelligence officials to receive a “detailed account” of what happened last weekend. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who on Wednesday held a meeting with union leaders organising marches, has vowed a “massive” police deployment for the fresh demonstrations called for Saturday by the Yellow Vest movement protesting rising inflation. The convulsion in France, the EU’s second-biggest economy after Germany, has rattled financial markets already nervous about the country’s growing debt pile and deficit. The yield on the French government’s benchmark 10-year bond has been rising, and on Wednesday surpassed five percent as investors demanded a higher return given the fiscal woes. A rising yield signifies a drop in bond prices. The Paris stock market also fell. On Friday, the Moody’s ratings agency is expected to lower its grade on France’s public debt. The country’s political landscape is so fragmented that Lecornu has little chance of winning swift parliamentary consensus for a cost-cutting budget that needs to be adopted before the end of this year. Le Pen leads race The latest survey, carried out by Ifop in the wake of the riots, suggested Le Pen would lead first-round voting intentions by a wide margin and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon emerged as her most likely opponent in the runoff. France’s neighbours Italy and Belgium have also started to experience similar unrest, on a smaller scale. Italy’s government has ordered 500 troops to Milan to stem street violence there. Macron said that “we don’t need a state of emergency” that would likewise permit soldiers to reinforce police against rioters, adding that “we have the means” already at authorities’ disposal, such as curfews. While the partial curfews have led to a calming of the situation in Paris and elsewhere, they have disrupted travel for commuters looking to take urban rail after 11pm (2am PKT). “It’s quite disconcerting,” said one Paris commuter who gave only his first name, Louis, when he found his line closed. But “if it can prevent further acts of vandalism… then yes, I think it’s a good thing”, he said. The Yellow Vest movement behind last weekend’s demonstrations announced on Wednesday that it had formally told authorities it planned to hold its Paris march on Saturday starting from Bastille square. The movement also wants to hold follow-up nationwide demonstrations on Nov 5. The images broadcast around the world of France’s street violence last weekend have prompted several countries, including the United States, China and Germany, to issue travel advisories for their citizens in France.

items.title: Gabon–Eswatini : Libreville mise sur le renforcement de la coopération Sud-Sud
items.description: Le vice-président de la République, Alexandre Barro Chambrier, a effectué une mission officielle au Royaume d’Eswatini du 18 au 20 octobre 2026. Porteur d’un message personnel du président Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema au roi Mswati III, il entend contribuer au renforcement des relations bilatérales et à l’ouverture de nouvelles perspectives de coopération. Photo de famille au terme de la rencontre. © Eswatini Government Le Gabon poursuit ses démarches de rapprochement avec les partenaires africains. À la tête d’une délégation comprenant notamment la ministre des Affaires étrangères, Marie-Édith Tassyla-Ye-Doumbeneny, le vice-président de la République, Alexandre Barro Chambrier, a séjourné du 18 au 20 octobre à Mbabane, capitale du Royaume d’Eswatini. Au cours de cette mission, le représentant gabonais a transmis au roi Mswati III un message personnel du chef de l’État, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema. Cette démarche diplomatique s’inscrit dans la volonté affichée de consolider les relations entre les deux pays et de donner davantage de substance à leur coopération. Alexandre Barro Chambrier et le roi Mswati III, en octobre 2026. © GabonReview (Capture d’écran) Au-delà du protocole, l’enjeu consiste à identifier des domaines dans lesquels les deux États pourraient développer des échanges et des partenariats. La coopération Sud-Sud offre, à cet égard, un cadre pour renforcer les relations politiques, favoriser les échanges économiques et partager des expériences en matière de développement. La position de l’Eswatini dans les instances régionales et continentales donne également une dimension diplomatique à cette démarche. Les consultations entre les autorités pourraient contribuer à rapprocher les positions des deux pays sur les questions d’intérêt commun. Toutefois, les retombées concrètes de cette visite dépendront de la traduction des intentions en projets précis. Des accords sectoriels, des mécanismes de suivi et des initiatives économiques permettraient de donner une portée opérationnelle à ce rapprochement. Pour Libreville, cette mission participe ainsi à une diplomatie de diversification des partenariats africains. Le défi sera désormais de faire émerger des coopérations mutuellement avantageuses, capables de dépasser les échanges institutionnels et de produire des résultats tangibles pour les deux populations. L’article Gabon–Eswatini : Libreville mise sur le renforcement de la coopération Sud-Sud est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Tivaouane Peulh–Niague : un centre commercial de deux milliards de FCfa inauguré
items.description: D'un coût global d'environ deux milliards de FCfa, le nouveau centre commercial « Tawfex » de Tivaouane Peulh–Niague a été officiellement réceptionné hier, mardi 20 octobre. Ce complexe marchand moderne marque une étape cruciale dans l'amélioration des conditions de travail des commerçants. La coordonnatrice nationale du Programme de modernisation et de gestion des marchés (Promogem), Rougui Aladji Sow, a procédé, hier, mardi 20 octobre, à la réception du centre commercial « Tawfex », sis à Tivaouane Peulh–Niague. Bâti sur 9.550 m², l’infrastructure offre, sur deux niveaux, des espaces commerciaux de nouvelle génération. Il est composé de 275 magasins, 40 toilettes, une salle de sport, un espace commercial pour la vente des fruits et légumes. A lire aussi : Réhabilitation de la route des Niayes: les riverains s’impatientent malgré un rythme des travaux jugé satisfaisant Estimé à près de deux milliards de FCfa, le centre dispose aussi de commodités modernes, notamment un bloc administratif, un espace de microfinance et une chambre froide. L’aboutissement de ce chantier marque une nouvelle étape pour le développement de l’économie locale. Selon Mme Sow, « cette infrastructure va améliorer les conditions de travail des commerçants, dynamiser le commerce local et participer favorablement au bien-être des populations locales ». Son érection est donc une réponse concrète à la modernisation des infrastructures marchandes. Cependant, la coordonnatrice nationale du Promogem a insisté sur la nécessité de l’entretenir. « Avec ce centre commercial moderne, nous traduisons la vision de l'État. Le défi actuel du Promogem n'est pas simplement de construire des murs et des bâtiments. Il s’agit de bâtir un véritable système de gestion qui garantira une gestion efficace, avec plus de sécurité et une bonne hygiène », a-t-elle souligné. Le maire de Tivaouane Peulh–Niague, Momar Sokhna Diop, a, pour sa part, magnifié le travail du Promogem qui, d’après lui, permet de transformer radicalement les espaces commerciaux. En plus de veiller à l’entretien de cet ouvrage, l’édile a exprimé la volonté de la municipalité de développer une bonne politique de suivi afin de garantir la durabilité de l’édifice. « Aujourd’hui, nous disposons d'un magnifique centre commercial et il nous incombe de le maintenir en parfait état pour le bien-être des populations. Le modèle de gestion choisi par le Promogem pour cette infrastructure nous convient pleinement et, ensemble, nous relèverons ces défis », a fait savoir le maire. Bada MBATHIE

items.title: Transavia et Volotea réduisent la voilure, Air Algérie passe à l’offensive
items.description: Après Transavia, la compagnie Volotea réduit discrètement sa voiture vers l’Algérie à partir de villes françaises pour la saison hivernale. Une aubaine pour Air Algérie qui renforce sa position sur le marché très lucratif des liaisons Algérie-France, et dans le même temps, elle lance une nouvelle offensive commerciale. La faible demande en saison hivernale et la hausse des coûts de kérosène incitent les compagnies aériennes à revoir la fréquence de leurs vols. La compagnie espagnole à bas prix Volotea a revu à la baisse son offre hivernale qui passe de 25 395 à 17 048 vols et de 4 362 216 à 2 915 028 sièges, rapporte le site spécialisé aeroroutes.com . Volotea réduit la fréquence de ses vols entre la France et l’Algérie Cette baisse de l’offre concerne plusieurs liaisons vers l’Algérie. La même source indique que le service Marseille-Béjaïa est annulé pour la période du 5 janvier au 18 février, Bordeaux-Oran est réduit de 63 à 44 vols, Lyon-Sétif de 97 à 86 vols, Marseille-Alger de 308 à 294, Marseille-Constantine de 75 à 66, Marseille-Oran de 254 à 139 et Marseille-Tlemcen de 20 à 17 vols. Enfin, le service Limoges – Oran est prolongé pendant la saison hivernale, avec un vol hebdomadaire aux dates suivantes : du 21 octobre 2026 au 6 janvier 2027 et du 18 février 2027 au 25 mars 2027. Transavia avait réduit ses vols de Montpellier vers Alger et Oran En septembre dernier, la compagnie néerlandaise Transavia a réduit sa voilure vers l’Algérie au départ de Montpellier à cause de la hausse des prix du kérosène. Sur la ligne Montpellier – Alger, Transavia ne propose que 4 vols pour ce mois d’octobre, 3 vols pour novembre, 3 vols pour décembre, 5 vols pour janvier 2027, 4 vols pour février 2027 et 3 vols pour mars 2027. Sur la liaison Montpellier – Oran, il est programmé un seul vol en octobre, 5 vols en novembre, 4 vols en décembre, 5 vols en janvier, 4 en février et 3 vols en mars 2027. Air Algérie lance sa promotion d’automne … Pendant que ces compagnies low-cost réduisent la fréquence de leurs vols, Air Algérie maintient tous ses programmes. La compagnie algérienne passe même à l’offensive avec le lancement de sa promotion spécial automne, prévoyant des réductions allant jusqu'à 50% sur les lignes internationales. La promotion a été lancée lundi 19 octobre. “L'automne vous réserve des offres exceptionnelles. Profitez de réductions allant jusqu'à 50 % sur les vols internationaux avec Air Algérie et faites de votre prochaine destination l'occasion de découvrir de nouveaux horizons”, a écrit la compagnie nationale sur ses réseaux sociaux. Air Algérie ouvre 6 nouvelles lignes en une semaine Air Algérie poursuit aussi l'extension de ses dessertes internationales et s’apprête à ouvrir six nouvelles lignes. Selon le site Air Plus News, la compagnie aérienne algérienne lancera à partir du 25 octobre les lignes Alger–Conakry avec une fréquence de 3 vols par semaine, Alger–Brazzaville (3 vols hebdomadaires), Alger–Lagos–Abuja (1 vol hebdomadaire), Alger–Shanghai (3 vols/semaine en A330-900neo), Alger–Koweït–Amman (1 vol/semaine) ainsi que la reprise de la fréquence quotidienne Alger–Doha après 7 mois d’interruption. L’article Transavia et Volotea réduisent la voilure, Air Algérie passe à l’offensive est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Water rationing, rubbish pile-up raise disease fears in Yemen's besieged Taiz
items.description: By Olivia Le Poidevin GENEVA/TAIZ, Yemen Oct 21 (Reuters) - Families have started rationing water in and around Yemen's Taiz city, where renewed fighting has disrupted fuel supplies and access to water systems serving 3 million people, aid groups and UN agencies said. Meanwhile, mounting piles of rubbish along major roads are raising fears of disease outbreaks in the city, Yemen's third-largest.

items.title: Ali Bongo : «Que nul ne compte sur mon silence ou sur mon retrait, pour faire ce qu’il veut de ce pays
items.description: Son retrait politique aurait été un gage attendu par les militaires pour asseoir leur pouvoir. C’est ce qu’affirme désormais Ali Bongo Ondimba, qui relie sa déclaration de septembre 2024 à sa résidence surveillée et à la détention de son épouse et de son fils. Dans une adresse aux militants du PDG, l’ancien président récuse ce renoncement et défend une ligne d’opposition. « Tout a une limite » : Ali Bongo dénonce un retrait politique contraint et fait du PDG sa ligne rouge.© GabonReview (capture d’écran GMT) « Les militaires attendaient de moi des gages pour asseoir leur maintien au pouvoir. Mon retrait de la vie politique devait en être un .» Dans une adresse, le 20 octobre, aux militants du Parti démocratique gabonais (PDG), Ali Bongo Ondimba livre sa version des circonstances qui l’ont conduit à annoncer son retrait politique en septembre 2024. Il présente cette déclaration comme une concession faite sous pression, alors que lui-même et ses proches étaient privés de liberté. « En septembre 2024, je n’étais pas libre. J’étais en résidence surveillée. Mon épouse et mon fils étaient retenus en captivité », affirme l’ancien chef de l’État. Il invoque ensuite sa situation familiale pour expliquer sa décision : « Que peut faire un époux ? Que peut faire un père ? Ces mots, je les ai prononcés dans ces circonstances-là, c’est-à-dire sous la contrainte . » Un renoncement qu’il récuse désormais Ali Bongo ne décrit pas de négociation précise ni ne nomme les responsables qui auraient exigé ce retrait. Mais il établit explicitement un lien entre la pression qu’il dit avoir subie, la détention de ses proches et les gages politiques attendus par les militaires. « Aujourd’hui je suis libre, et ma parole aussi », poursuit-il, avant de déclarer : « Je ne renonce pas à la vie politique . » Il invoque son statut d’ancien président de la République et ses responsabilités envers le pays et son parti pour justifier sa prise de parole. « Que nul ne compte sur mon silence ou sur mon retrait, pour faire ce qu’il veut de ce pays, ou disposer du parti. Mon devoir n’est pas terminé . » Il répond également aux militants qui avaient vécu son silence comme un abandon : « Le contexte m’empêchait de parler, et je vous dirai pourquoi » Une adresse à la nation est annoncée « dans les tout prochains jours ». Le retrait de septembre au cœur du conflit au PDG Cette explication sert aussi sa contestation de la direction actuelle du PDG. Ali Bongo reproche aux responsables du parti d’avoir invoqué sa déclaration de septembre 2024 pour justifier des décisions remontant au mois de mars précédent. Selon son récit, la rencontre du 7 mars 2024 à sa résidence devait permettre d’assurer la continuité du parti, sans remettre en cause sa présidence. « Je n’avais ni démissionné, ni autorisé une direction en dehors de nos règles », soutient-il. Il affirme avoir adressé une mise en demeure aux dirigeants actuels, puis invité Blaise Louembé et deux camarades à Paris pour rechercher une sortie de crise. « Ils ne sont pas venus. Ils n’ont pas répondu à mon appel », déclare-t-il. Il revendique la conduite d’une réorganisation transitoire et appelle les militants à ne pas cautionner « un congrès unilatéral ». L’opposition comme cap, le parti comme limite Sur l’orientation politique, Ali Bongo défend une rupture avec le soutien au pouvoir : « Nous avons perdu le pouvoir. Notre place est donc logiquement dans l’opposition . » Il précise que le congrès décidera de l’orientation du parti, mais défend déjà une ligne d’indépendance : « Le PDG ne sera la béquille de personne. Ni alliance de façade, ni fusion, ni absorption . » L’ancien président explique également pourquoi il n’a pas résisté au coup d’État : « Je n’ai pas voulu que le sang des Gabonais coule pour une affaire de pouvoir . » Une retenue qu’il oppose à sa détermination à défendre son parti : « Mais ma patience n’est pas de la faiblesse. Tout a une limite. Cette limite, c’est le Parti Démocratique Gabonais . » Aux acteurs extérieurs qu’il accuse de vouloir contrôler le PDG, il adresse un avertissement : « Je n’ai pas réagi au coup d’État. Je ne laisserai personne s’emparer du PDG. Arrêtez-vous là . » Il se dit prêt à « tous les sacrifices », en précisant : « par toutes les voies que la loi et la démocratie nous ouvrent ». Son retrait récusé, Ali Bongo entend désormais faire de sa parole retrouvée un instrument de reconquête politique. L’article Ali Bongo : «Que nul ne compte sur mon silence ou sur mon retrait, pour faire ce qu’il veut de ce pays est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Egypt Forum 2026 celebrates higher attendance at schools still struggling without teachers or classrooms
items.description: Education has remained one of the main domestic fronts for the government in recent years, with chronic complaints around low spending in the sector. At the start of the academic year in September, Education Minister Mohamed Abdel Latif faced fierce public and parliamentary pushback over controversial decisions affecting schools nationwide. Chief among them was the new enforcement of compulsory weekly assessments and homework, along with curriculum shakeups that drew formal parliamentary briefing requests accusing the ministry of running an evaluation regime that burns out students and teachers — who are already scarce — without improving learning. Amid this simmering backlash, the Cabinet scrambled to stage-manage the narrative ahead of Egypt Forum 2026, a multi-day event mandated by President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on October 1 to showcase national development and institutional dialogue. After opening a window for people to register questions and concerns for discussion at the forum, the Cabinet said that education had outpaced all other issues with more than 15,000 public inquiries submitted on the topic, reflecting the degree of public concern. We don’t know what these public inquiries were, as they have not been published in a publicly accessible location so far. So, what did the government choose to talk about? In line with the presidency’s official “ human development ” agenda, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbuly announced earlier this month that basic education would anchor the forum’s flagship opening session under the title: “What Do Our Children Learn… and Does It Prepare Them for the Future?” Decision-makers and policy experts at the forum framed a discussion of education policy around the central question of whether current curricula adequately prepare students for future labor market demands. But after the display of a video on education “ challenges and achievements ” which Mada Masr was not able to review, the forum proceeded on Monday with the minister outlining a set of achievements leading with huge improvements in school attendance — a fact presented as a fait accompli that would allow the government’s policy focus to transition “from expanding basic school access, to ensuring actual learning quality,” as one of the session aims stated. Mada Masr looked into the claim that school attendance and access has improved enough to allow for improvements to learning quality, exploring government data and statements, and speaking with the education program coordinator at the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights. What we found is that at least part of the boost in attendance is driven by the most recent curriculum change: increased regular testing, which is an innovation that the government says is improving learning, despite complaints about the approach from families and MPs who say it increases the strain on teachers and students without improving educational outcomes, as well as conflicting with recommended educational approaches in pedagogical research. We also looked into the government’s ambitious target to improve learning by reducing classroom density and canceling school “evening shifts,” finding that these aims will be difficult to implement without radical changes to how it is currently handling the major deficit in classroom provision and teacher hiring. *** Speaking at the forum on Monday, the education minister laid out numbers to demonstrate improvements in the last decade to children’s access to government schools — attended by 80 percent of Egyptian pupils. Abdel Latif said attendance rates stood at just 15 percent in the 2023/24 academic year, but have risen exponentially to reach 87 percent for the following school year. The dramatic improvement was celebrated in May by the head of education at UNICEF Egypt, Shiraz Chakera, who cited a new study on Egypt’s educational reforms from 2024 to 2026 in a conference with the government. And the number is still going up, the minister asserted at the forum, saying the attendance rate has risen from 87 percent to 90 percent for the current school year. These figures appear positive. But they don’t tell us who is attending school and why. Mada Masr looked into the numbers to understand if the higher attendance represents real improvement in quality across pre-university education, and tried to understand where the change has come from and whether it indicates a strong base for the curriculum reforms the government is looking to focus on. Regular testing keeps pupils in school, but is it improving learning? High attendance in the primary and preparatory stages is not new. In 2021, 93 percent of children aged 6 to 11 were already attending school, and only 3.4 per cent of primary school age children were “out-of-school,” or 3.6 per cent of preparatory school age children, according to the Egyptian Family Health Survey, whose data was cited by UNICEF in a 2024 report. Attendance has historically been less strong for secondary school age children. The same study put the percentage of children of secondary school age who don’t go to school at almost four times higher than at primary school age, at 12.2 per cent, or around 1.4 million children. But in general, head of the education program at EIPR Mohamed Sayed agreed that there is a marked improvement in primary and secondary school attendance. Speaking to Mada Masr, the researcher put improved attendance down, in part, to the compulsory regular testing that has been introduced alongside the new Egyptian Baccalaureate program launched this year as an alternative to the traditional thanaweya amma Through the program, the Education Ministry has codified regular assessments into high school graduation requirements. Education Ministerial Decree 150/2026, published in the Official Gazette on October 15, says that Egyptian Baccalaureate students must get at least 60 percent on weekly and monthly evaluations in each subject to be eligible to take graduation exams in their last two years of secondary school. Sayed noted that while the exams may have supported a boost in secondary school attendance, the regular testing is something that parents and teachers have complained places children and teachers under undue stress. Abdel Latif further defended on Monday the weekly assessments, homework and monthly tests as essential tools used internationally to monitor student understanding, citing their global adoption to justify the policy. But the system has faced domestic pushback, with critics arguing that it fails to improve learning outcomes while placing an undue burden on both students and teachers. In the days leading up to the forum, two MPs filed separate parliamentary briefing requests about intensive testing in school curricula. MP Nashwa al-Sherif said students should have enough time to understand and review their lessons without being under constant pressure over grades, according to news reports, while MP Amal Asfour said that tying grades to attendance, or using assessments as a means of disciplining or pressuring children, could negatively affect their relationship with school. Modern international educational trends have also increasingly shifted away from excessive testing, favoring approaches that afford teachers and students greater flexibility to focus on deep learning. For instance, a prominent semi-national language school in downtown Cairo recently held a back-to-school orientation where the pedagogical team emphasized a reduced-testing philosophy in meeting notes distributed to parents and reviewed by Mada Masr . According to the meeting notes, the French curriculum for the French Baccalaureat operates on multi-year learning cycles rather than a strict annual framework, relying on continuous assessment to track progress instead of high-stakes examinations that place pressure on students. The pedagogical focus is on skills, contrasting with the traditional system’s emphasis on rote knowledge and uniform teaching methods. The international track also embeds the “right to make mistakes” and encourages progressive student autonomy under less directive supervision, allowing grade advancement within cycles without mandatory end-of-year exams. Attendance growth outstrips classroom capacity With the improved school attendance relying on extensive testing, schools which were already struggling with few classrooms and even fewer teachers now have a greater number of pupils and extra workload for teachers to grapple with. The minister’s focus on increased attendance glossed over the compounding deficits in the number of classrooms and in teaching capacity that are documented in the government’s own records. He estimated in 2024 a shortfall of about 250,000 classrooms, resulting in serious classroom overcrowding. “Some of the classrooms had 100 or 150 students,” he said during the forum, citing Al-Marg and Khanka as some examples. But now, “there isn’t a class with over 50 students in it,” he claimed, adding that in future, “we have a vision to reduce the density to 40 and 45 students in one classr oom.” How can the ministry achieve this ambition? So far, its rate of classroom building has been much slower than what is needed to reduce classroom density in a meaningful way, based on the figures Mada Masr reviewed. According to publicly available data in the ministry’s ‘ yearbook ,’ there were 435,308 government school classrooms during the 2019/20 academic year. This number increased to 591,217 classes for the academic year 2024/25. As per Mada Masr’s calculations, based on the ministry’s data over that period, the increase in the number of government school classrooms happened as follows: 6,477 new classrooms were added in the 2020/21 academic year 16,115 in 2021/22 5,271 in 2022/23 777 in 2023/24 127,269 in 2024/25 But not all of these classrooms represent newly built additions. The minister said on Monday that 150,000 new classrooms have been added over the past ten years at a cost exceeding LE200 billion. The ministry spokesperson has also said in recent months that since Adbel Latif became minister, 98,000 of the new classrooms have come from “introducing” new school rooms for use in classes. This has relied on re-utilizing existing rooms in schools, the spokesperson explained, alongside the policy to reduce classroom density by splitting classroom use between evening and morning school “shifts.” But now, alongside the ambitious target to reduce classroom density down to 40-45 students, the minister also announced on Monday a major target to stop running school evening shifts by 2029. How the government aims to both reduce classroom density and end the evening shifts with no plan to increase the number of available rooms is unclear. Abdel Latif announced no additional spending plan to build new classrooms in line with the plan to cancel the evening shifts. Discounting the 98,000 “introduced” clasrooms from the figures on classroom additions for the past five years, the figures show an average increase in school classrooms of around 11,581 classrooms per year over the past five years. At this average rate of government classroom addition per year, it would take over 10 years to plug the gap of 250,000 missing classrooms identified by the ministry in 2024, even if we subtract from the target the classrooms added in the 2024/25 academic year, including the 98,000 reutilized classrooms. And teachers are still left at the bottom of the barrel As well as no policy plan to increase classrooms, Abdel Latif also neglected to announce how the government will address the urgent teachers shortage. Teachers are one of the main victims of the Education Ministry’s unwillingness to spend on its policies. With strict regulations on hiring in the public sector, the ministry has acknowledged the huge gap in the number of teachers available. Abdel Latif pointed to the ongoing deficit on Monday, saying that the public education system faces an estimated deficit of more than 469,000 teachers, with a current teaching force of 832,000. Still, hiring remains limited to around 30,000 teachers per year on the basis of annual “competitions” that slowly rule out applicants based on criteria including physical fitness and weight, as Mada Masr documented in 2022. One of the applicants said at the time that they had “passed all the tests related to academic and educational specialization, general culture, computer use and proficiency in English,” but had failed a round of physical testing hosted at the Military Academy where their height and weight were recorded, and they were asked to do push ups, sit ups and jumps. High competition for positions and frustration with the weight-based discrimination saw hundreds of teachers protest the ministry’s hiring decisions at the end of the competition. Additional hiring competitions, launched last year, seek to offer assistant teacher contracts to teachers currently working per-class. 11,693 appointments were advertised last year, with a new initiative this year to hire the per-class teachers. But if the number of teachers hired per year remains around 40,000 — between granting contracts to per-class teachers and the hiring competitions — it will take the government 11 years to fill the 469,000 positions that Abdel Latif said are needed *** This report is published as part of the joint campaign with eight media platforms in solidarity with the detained Matsda2sh journalists.
